This design therefore accepts possible extra cross-node query work and promises no equivalent performance. Verify exact version capabilities. CREATE GLOBAL INDEX, official query-plan example. Design consequences: - Ordinary indexes provide neither cross-DN global uniqueness nor GSI's separate distribution/covering design; changing an index does not redistribute its base table. - Retaining indexed columns does not preserve query plans, covering behavior, or JOIN performance. Validate representative queries with EXPLAIN . - A global structure required to enforce PK identity cannot be relaxed. Prefer distribution compatible with the PK. Stop before table creation when correctness cannot be preserved. - An explicitly global primary index or a GSI on the exact primary or candidate identity columns requires a distribution plan, even when the columns are reordered. A business GSI with additional columns can still become an ordinary index. A plain UNIQUE on exactly the declared identity columns retains uniqueness. - Existing GSI may support constraints or other dependencies. Migration must inspect ownership, dependencies, validity, and rollback paths before removal. Partition GLOBAL/LOCAL indexes describe partition coverage and must not be confused with distributed GSI. openGauss partition-index syntax is not evidence of GaussDB GSI capability. openGauss index documentation. Distributed business and metadata tables Relaxing business secondary constraints does not remove restrictions involving PKs, distribution/partition columns, or types. Distribution planning must be deterministic, explainable, and overridable, with an explicit write strategy for PK/distribution-key changes. Metadata requires its own design: deduplication keys, task IDs, stream ordering, and lease operations must satisfy distributed constraints, while business changes and local target checkpoints remain atomic. Do not delete UNIQUE(job id, transaction key) to avoid GSI, or infer source ordering from independent CN-generated IDs. The current metadata layout has not been validated on commercial distributed GaussDB and is not a deployment template for it. Planning and resumable execution Implementation requires these steps, not merely removing a UNIQUE keyword: 1. Discover source index metadata: PK/secondary classification, column order, prefix lengths, expressions, sort direction, visibility, and method. Persist a versioned conversion manifest. 2. Generate executable DDL and capability differences for the target product/version/mode, distribution/partitioning, and types. Deduplicate equivalent target indexes; use stable digests when shortening names. 3. Create columns and PKs before snapshot; persist definitions, policy, and fingerprints. Correct row identity comes first. 4. Prefer ordinary business secondary-index creation after initial catch-up, with bounded concurrency. CDC progress and index readiness are separate: streaming does not imply every index is READY. 5. Persist planned/started/succeeded/failed states and definition digests per target/table/index. After restart, inspect catalog definitions and validity before proceeding. Adapter-specific recovery must cover nontransactional DDL and invalid indexes left by online builds. 6. A matching name with a different definition is not success. Retain diagnostics and retry the object without resetting snapshot cursors or skipping business transactions. Pause a target if DDL failure compromises safe writes; a missing acceleration-only index may instead leave CDC running with a failed index phase. Report prefix, expression, FULLTEXT, SPATIAL, invisible, oversized, and unsupported-collation indexes individually. Initially automate only ordinary column-based B-tree-like indexes; explicitly list other objects as unsupported/manual work rather than claiming complete index synchronization. Do not silently expand a prefix index to the full column, which may exceed limits or change plans. Application takeover This is a planned operating procedure, not an existing automated command. Validate each target independently; simultaneous takeover of every target is unnecessary: 1. Freeze relevant source business writes and DDL; record a final source GTID barrier and eliminate dual-write entry points. 2. Wait for the target to apply through that barrier with no failed transactions, missing logs, or unfinished snapshot. Use proven target application progress, not shared capture GTID alone. 3. At the same frozen boundary, compare row counts, PK sets, chunk digests/required row values, and semantics for restored constraints. Retain original UNIQUE definitions in the conversion manifest. 4. Validate duplicates, NULLs, lengths, and dependencies using actual target equality rules; build required UNIQUE/FK constraints. If distributed constraints need GSI or redistribution, plan and validate that separately. Ordinary indexes during synchronization do not justify omitting constraints permanently after takeover. 5. Once all required constraints are valid and checks pass, stop or fence synchronization writes to that target, then permit application writes. Failure blocks takeover; repair and retry without deleting conflicting rows to force success. After application writes begin, the original one-way sync service cannot safely overwrite that target without coordination. Failback or bidirectional replication requires a separate design; GTID retention does not provide it. Other mirror targets may retain their own subscriptions, but after business moves to the new database the original MySQL source does not automatically receive those new writes. FAQ Will retries insert extra rows without UNIQUE? The keyed design uses PKs and transaction checkpoints; an ordinary email index does not deduplicate. No-PK support is now a first-release requirement but remains unimplemented. It needs candidate identity or consistent-baseline/multiset handling, not the keyed guarantee; see platform design. Are repeated email values always errors? No. Distinguish NULLs, comparison differences, and pre-catch-up mixed scan states. Judge against source definitions at a declared boundary; do not automatically delete rows. Are ordinary indexes always faster than GSI? No. They may reduce write maintenance but increase the DNs visited by queries. Measure actual workloads. Will existing target UNIQUE indexes change automatically? No. Current code does not do this; the design first produces an object/dependency migration plan. Constraint-owned indexes are not standalone objects to DROP blindly. Does an interrupted index build restart the snapshot? The design retains data checkpoints and resumes index work after catalog inspection. Implementation and fault validation remain pending. Is constraint restoration guaranteed to succeed? No. Actual validation and constraint creation gate takeover. Incompatible distribution/constraints or inconsistent data must block it. Acceptance checklist - Single/composite UNIQUE becomes nonunique with traceable ordering, nullability, and conversion manifests; PK/internal uniqueness remains intact. - Temporary email duplicates during online scans converge to the frozen source boundary; updates, deletes, PK changes, and transaction redelivery preserve rows. - Validate independently lagging targets; index failure on one target must not corrupt another target's state. - Test process death around index DDL, connection loss, uncertain responses, definition conflicts, invalid indexes, and stale owners. - Use real multi-CN/DN GaussDB to validate distribution compatibility, global row identity, transaction ordering, and ordinary-index plans; validate openGauss separately. - Before takeover, validate collations, empty strings/NULLs, target uniqueness, and the frozen barrier. Deliberate conflicts must block switching without discarding data. For commercial acceptance, record the distributed GaussDB build, compatibility mode, GTM mode, CN/DN topology and JDBC driver. In a disposable database, run the real sink against a plain business UNIQUE(email) , a modeled business GSI, a GSI on reordered composite identity columns and an explicitly global primary index. Use JDBC catalog metadata to verify that both business plans create nonunique ordinary indexes with the planned names and column order. Verify that both identity GSI cases stop before table creation. Capture EXPLAIN for representative lookups on the declared distribution. Then disconnect and replay, and check primary-key enforcement and the sink checkpoint together. GaussDB CREATE GLOBAL INDEX · GaussDB GSI query-plan example The current validation record excludes these new capabilities. It must not be used to claim index conversion or commercial distributed GaussDB acceptance. Doris business UNIQUE/GSI conversion uses nonunique inverted indexes; its internal UNIQUE KEY protects source row identity only. This is not GaussDB B-tree equivalence and does not preserve business uniqueness, collation or global routing. See the Doris handbook.

title: GBase 8c
text: GBase 8c destination GBASE 8C is an experimental adapter using the vendor's com.gbase8c.Driver and jdbc:gbase8c:// . 8a, 8c and 8s are separate product families ; PostgreSQL wire compatibility does not establish support for all three. 8a/8s remain separate planned adapters. The first profile targets V6 S1.3.0B19 ARM64, PG/UTF8; the first actual MySQL+PostgreSQL mixed snapshot/CDC/TIME/keyless/text-key/outage/catch-up/worker-kill/SQL-repair/missing-table acceptance passed. This applies to that profile and is not a full production matrix claim. See config/gbase8c-v3.yml. CLI and the Web v3 wizard share this adapter. Pre-create a PG-compatible UTF8 database and a synchronization account allowed to create schemas/tables/indexes and execute DML. The service does not change global compatibility settings or promote database nodes. Use a separate login. Native tests confirmed that initialization owner omm cannot connect remotely, and CREATEDB alone does not authorize schema creation inside postgres . An administrator can grant the required database scope: Existing schemas/tables need their own permissions or ownership. Synchronization does not require SYSADMIN. The fixture's CREATEDB attribute exists to create a negative compatibility-mode test database; pre-created production databases do not require copying that attribute. See the vendor permission guide. Session and data contract Every physical connection checks the metadata product and actual kernel version before vendor-specific SQL. It requires PG mode, UTF8, preserved empty strings and case/trailing-space-sensitive text comparisons. It sets session UTC, synchronous local commit and standard string escaping. Read-only endpoints raise a retryable connection error. Other compatibility modes require separate semantic and type plans. Quoted identifiers, row tables and primary keys are used. Keyless rows have internal occurrence IDs. JSON maps to JSONB; UINT64 to DECIMAL(20,0), wide decimals retain precision, binary maps to BYTEA, timestamps retain microseconds, and MySQL TIME becomes a signed INTERVAL. Generated values are taken from the source; complete target-side expression reconstruction is not promised. A native probe confirmed VARCHAR(100) holds 100 four-byte Unicode characters. Business changes and the target checkpoint share a local transaction and epoch fence. One unavailable target does not prevent independent targets acknowledging data. This does not imply cross-target distributed atomicity or protection against arbitrary physical backup rollback, split brain or external business writers. Index and distributed scope DOWNGRADE BUSINESS turns non-identity business UNIQUE into ordinary indexes. Simple business GSI conversion loses global uniqueness and routing. Primary, identity and internal uniqueness cannot be downgraded. Existing UNIQUE is not automatically dropped; expression/prefix/full-text/spatial indexes need a reviewed plan. Only the synchronization service may write destination business tables; validate and restore constraints before takeover. Distributed tables add distribution-key and unique-constraint restrictions: see the vendor SQL reference. A single-instance PG acceptance cannot establish CN/DN, DSS shared-storage, HA failover, cross-shard transaction or redistribution compatibility. Distribution-key changes, metadata/ownership placement, preserved UNIQUE and global indexes require independent planning and native verification. Recovery and FAQ - On downtime/network failure, retain journal/checkpoints and wait for the same writable destination. Size retained logs and source binlog retention for the outage. - SQL errors pause the affected subscription. Inspect/fix the cause and resume the original transaction. Manual skip/compensating data editing is not implemented. - Missing business tables isolate the affected target. Do not edit checkpoints; rebuilding or resnapshotting requires a separate plan. - Arbitrary nonempty adoption is rejected. Empty existing tables still need column/key/trigger/FK/index/ownership validation. - Unsupported live source DDL pauses safely; complete online schema evolution is pending. - The vendor filename is gbase8c-jdbc-3.0.0B02.jar , its embedded Maven version is 3.0.0 , and runtime DriverVersion contains an unresolved placeholder. Exact input identity uses fixed filenames and SHA-256, not that version string. Reproducible inputs Vendor downloads. Driver ZIP SHA-256: 3c2645993cd2e20a19941fc4d4bb5aba0f02ca378766543b6dd259a50c382721 ; JAR SHA-256: fe115f05124f6b9f37e49c829a0def28f7d09a6d871dd62a0c9f856b0aaa7e91 . The build verifies both, preserves vendor classes and a dedicated license resource, and checks Java 8-compatible bytecode. Native fixtures use separately obtained lawful vendor binaries. No database binaries/licenses are distributed in the repository. The local base image in tests/gbase8c/Dockerfile supplies Linux userland; the actual executable is verified vendor gbased , not openGauss pretending to be GBase. 中文 Native fixture reproduction / 原生夹具复现 Use Python 3.12+ and a lawful matching ARM64 vendor installer: Installer SHA-256: 6946abaa7666cbfadea3957682020262a102e52c6f7b4632d1f93fee9d3400b7 ; extracted B19 kernel SHA-256: 69663acfbb786c3f05cc434fb9f6d42806609b69c818c6e6ce0c4234748ad582 , matching its vendor checksum. The unified installer also contains a B10 kernel; this fixture explicitly selects B19.

title: Global task control
text: Global task control: activation, recovery and limits 中文 2026-11-17: an optional fixed-owner global profile now wires public HTTP, UI, shared configuration, durable commands and remote reads. Local control remains the default. CP-02/03 remain PARTIAL: legacy task import, complete business workflows, capacity and fault matrices are not fully accepted. Automatic owner relocation is separate. Activation Members share the control database, cluster.id, namespace, sharedAccess=true, sharedTasks=true and taskKey. Each has a distinct stable nodeId and private persistent task/data directories. taskKey is canonical Base64 text encoding 32 random bytes, supplied through protected environment configuration. Keep it out of task YAML. Never share controller.json. First activation requires empty task directories; existing registered tasks or YAML fail with GLOBAL TASK IMPORT REQUIRED. There is no automatic legacy import tool yet. Theplatform examplesupports Linux. Follow thefirst-release baseline;node modes,identities and keys must agree. Mode mismatches refuse without automatic migration or local fallback. Supply database credentials, token, key and node ID through the deployment environment. The example enables Secure cookies: expose HTTPS and configure the correct publicOrigin at the proxy. Helm and native Kubernetes The global Helm values reference existing Secrets: token in rivomesh-auth, and username/password/task-key in rivomesh-control-store. task-key contains the same Base64 key text on all members. Use separate releases, private PVCs and stable node IDs: Alternatively adapt and apply the native manifests A and B with kubectl apply -f. Independent controllers must not share a private directory. Static Helm/native parity and invalid-configuration checks exist; live Kubernetes/CSI, node-fault and rolling-upgrade acceptance remain open. Docker uses the same independent persistent-directory and key requirements. Acceptance fixtures leave no persistent preview. UI and configuration The session field taskControlScope=GLOBAL identifies this profile. Any entry lists authorized tasks with cursor pagination, owner/node state, global revision, Worker state, desired/active configuration and command results. Creation and import allow a specific execution node or automatic assignment. Import creates a new task. Unavailable owner execution is UNKNOWN, not stopped. Create/edit/restore/actions return 202 for durable admission only. Configuration history separates desired/active; the active pointer advances after successful owner application. Failed proposals preserve the old active configuration. Masked secret references work across entries. Connection previews, raw differences and repair-plan reads use expiring owner queries and require the owner to be online. Global maximumTasks/maximumCommands differ from per-node maxTasks/maxRunningTasks. Defaults are 10000 global tasks and 1000 active commands; configuration ranges are resource guards, not hardware throughput promises. Queries are limited to 512KiB requests, 1MiB responses, 1–60 second lifetime, bounded readers and retained capacity. Filter the shared task list by exact task ID or execution node ID. Both filters also work together. GET /api/tasks?ownerNodeId=agent-a&taskId=orders&limit=20 applies account grants and the requested filters before computing the total or next page. Keep the same filters when using after . Within a task select a destination to isolate its state, SQL error and pending journal transactions. The count is the difference between captured and safely covered sequence at the observation time. Stale observations hide this count. Consumer completion requires its own measurement. Evidence In Diagnostics , administrators can switch from Source capture to an individual destination. The scoped endpoint is GET /api/tasks/orders/diagnostics?subscriptionId=warehouse&limit=20 . It returns recent destination pauses, retries and cleared retries with observation timestamps. Capture and destination events have separate rotating files in the execution Agent's private log directory. Destination files share two 64 KiB segments per task. Events can expire during heavy fault activity. Keep the same destination when using after . Error text, SQL, row values and credentials are excluded. A cleared retry records the Worker’s recovery observation. Check the destination's acknowledged sequence and pending count for delivery progress. Each Agent shares a budget of eight diagnostics pages per second across its Controller entries, with an initial burst of 16 pages. On HTTP 429 with DIAGNOSTICS RATE LIMITED , use the Retry-After header and retry the original cursor. Each page carries at most 25 events. Other task status reads and control commands have their own request paths. For PostgreSQL sources and transactional SQL destinations, the task status field lastDeliveryTiming shows the last verifiable sample for each destination. It compares the source commit timestamp on the logical replication wire with the time the Worker observed the destination return from commit. It includes transport time and assumes the source and Worker clocks agree. Synchronize those clocks. If the Worker sees the destination complete before the source timestamp, the API reports CLOCK SKEW without a duration. Both timestamps are UTC. Delay in whole milliseconds and the journal sequence are decimal strings. PostgreSQL logical replication message formats The sample belongs to a specific confirmed transaction. During a pause, retry or backlog, the console labels it historical. Before the first sample or when a newer acknowledgment lacks a direct observation, it reports UNKNOWN . Empty projections, snapshots, barriers, skips and reconciliation after an uncertain commit do not produce a sample. Run status, pending count and contiguous delivery progress describe the current task. The latest sample survives Worker restarts and collection of its original log entry. The same measurement is available for direct MySQL 8.4 writes when source.expectedVersion is set to "8.4" or an exact 8.4 patch release. Use a local or external journal without writer assignment and a transactional SQL destination. The sample uses the standard GTID event's original commit timestamp in microseconds, verified against the connected writer's identity and version. The source must have originated the write and report the same original and immediate timestamps. Relayed transactions, older binlogs, missing timestamp metadata, Group Replication and writer-assignment journals report UNKNOWN . Group Replication records its original timestamp when the transaction is ready for certification. MySQL replication delay timestamps · GTID event format Automatic assignment for new tasks In the create wizard or YAML import, select Assign an Agent automatically . The control store chooses an authorized, live Agent with task capacity. It compares assigned tasks as a share of each Agent's maxTasks and reserves the chosen slot in the same transaction that persists the task. Use placement: "AUTO" with POST /api/tasks , the configuration and an X-Request-ID . To choose a specific Agent, send ownerNodeId . For V3 tasks with a MySQL or PostgreSQL source, MySQL or PostgreSQL destinations and an external PostgreSQL journal, automatic placement checks up to three eligible Agents in capacity order. Each Agent checks its Java 21 Worker launcher and the components required by the source, destinations and journal, then opens the configured journal with a bounded read-only SELECT 1 . Connector/J is required when MySQL is the source or a destination. Only MySQL sources require the binlog reader. A failed candidate does not acquire the task. If all candidates fail, AGENT PLACEMENT UNAVAILABLE leaves the global task and journal unchanged. Fix the Agent's driver, credential or journal route and repeat the create request. This check confirms journal authentication at the time of placement. Use Check connections and objects on the saved task to inspect its source and destinations. Other connector and journal profiles still use the existing capacity-based placement rules. The saved task lists its actual owner. Repeating the accepted request ID and configuration from either Controller returns that owner even if the cluster has since filled its task slots. Assess transfer to another Agent In the task details, select Assess Agent handoff . Choose a candidate from the node directory and record the assessment. The dialog shows the candidate's registry status and the recorded blockers. Select Refresh nodes and assessment to read current information from either entry. If a submission outcome is unknown, Retry the same assessment preserves its request ID and inputs. If another entry saved a newer assessment, review that receipt before recording a replacement. An administrator can record a handoff assessment from either Controller. Send POST /api/tasks/ id /handoff with an X-Request-ID and a JSON body containing candidateNodeId and the task's expectedRevision . GET /api/tasks/ id /handoff reads the current assessment. To refresh it, send a new request ID and set expectedAssessment to the current assessment ID. Retrying the current request with its original inputs returns the same assessment. Both Agents and the task must be in the caller's scope. The assessment binds the task revision and active configuration, the two Agent registrations, candidate task capacity and the original Agent's observed capture position. It checks for outstanding commands and a complete, acknowledged cut on a supported MySQL source with a PostgreSQL external journal and PostgreSQL or MySQL targets. A change in the observed cut, pending work, Agent registration or available capacity marks the assessment STALE . Its checkpoint is represented by a digest. The response excludes source positions, credentials and private recovery files. EVIDENCE REQUIRED means these control-plane checks passed. The candidate must still prove connectivity and access to the original recovery reports and receipts. BLOCKED identifies earlier prerequisites such as an active Worker or exhausted task capacity. Assessment leaves the task owner, Worker, capacity reservations and journal unchanged. The response carries executionAuthorized: false . Send POST /api/tasks/ id /handoff/probe with expectedAssessment to ask the currently enrolled candidate to verify the original journal generation, MySQL GTID history and native PostgreSQL/MySQL target receipts. The request uses the candidate's own connection settings and secret resolution. The two read-only queries expire within 30 seconds and verify the task revision and both Agent enrollments again on completion. The latest assessment retains the sanitized result. A stale or replaced assessment requires a refresh before probing again. The original Agent reports presence of its private validation, source and failure evidence directories and its retained operation receipt count. This inventory leaves private custody with the original Agent and reports ORIGINAL PRIVATE EVIDENCE CUSTODY UNPROVEN . Successful candidate verification clears the connectivity blocker while fresh. The result still carries executionAuthorized: false . To verify custody of completed validation reports, mount the same private storage on both Agents and set cluster.handoffEvidenceRoot to the existing absolute path on each Agent. Use owner-only POSIX permissions and an execution identity that can access the mount. The original Agent needs write access and the candidate needs read access. The mount must support file locks and atomic same-directory rename. Earlier tasks and installations continue to use their original report directories. For Helm, set cluster.handoffEvidenceClaim to the same existing ReadWriteMany PVC in both Agent releases. Set each release's persistence.existingClaim to its own initialized private state PVC. The chart mounts the shared claim at /app/handoff-evidence and passes that path to Rivomesh. Prepare both volumes for the Agent's UID and GID 10001 . The shared claim root requires mode 0700 . This profile omits Pod fsGroup so Kubernetes preserves the filesystem permissions. Kubernetes volume permissions For native Kubernetes YAML, add the existing shared PVC to each Agent Deployment and mount it at /app/handoff-evidence . Keep each Agent's own state PVC mounted at /app/data . Omit spec.template.spec.securityContext.fsGroup for this profile and set cluster.handoffEvidenceRoot: /app/handoff-evidence in each Agent ConfigMap. Roll out the updated Agents after preparing the two volumes. During a probe, the original Agent locks each completed report and exports the exact rows.mv.db and summary.json bytes. Each attempt handles up to 32 reports within a shared 64 MiB payload budget for reports and historical failure evidence. The scoped archive replaces the previous export for that original task only after a complete write. The candidate verifies the archive digest, assessment, task revision and both Agent directory identities. probe.sharedReportCustody reports the result, file size and digest. The protected mount holds the report data. Original archives, signing keys and repair plans remain under the original Agent’s private state. The probe preserves task ownership and returns executionAuthorized: false . The same probe can verify closed operation receipts through probe.sharedReceiptCustody . The original Agent matches the signed global command history against its private request signatures, actors and outcomes. It archives only these closed records and the candidate checks their exact bytes in the scoped archive. This first profile covers up to 64 global commands for the selected task. A missing, pruned, mismatched or unresolved local receipt keeps custody unproven. The response contains counts and digests. Receipt import and transfer authorization require separate verification. probe.sharedFailureEvidenceCustody reports custody of up to 64 historical failure records. Under the original store lock, the original Agent verifies the authority scope and the HMAC and content digest of every retained record. The archive contains their exact authority and record bytes. The original Agent keeps the signing key. The candidate verifies the archive digest received over the authenticated owner route, the assessment scope, and the number and shape of archived entries. Missing authority, a changed record, or a busy store prevents the original Agent from publishing that export. The response exposes counts, size and digest. Using a preserved record for recovery requires the original authorization and key. probe.sharedRawCaptureCustody verifies authenticated MySQL binlog archives through a separate private ZIP. Under the native archive lock, the original Agent verifies its HMAC receipt for each retained file and checks the exact file locator, byte count, digest and original owner. It exports the full raw file and its receipt. The candidate obtains the scoped ZIP digest through the authenticated Agent route, then verifies both archive and per-file digests and sizes. Each task can include up to 64 raw archives under a separate 64 MiB budget. A mixed store with unbound files, missing receipts or changed bytes fails source custody while leaving the separate report archive intact. The original Agent provides authenticity with its private key. Controllers expose only custody status, counts, size and digest. The ZIP is limited to verification, with transfer execution subject to separate fencing and approval. When both Agents verify the exact stopped cut and the original closed receipts, the assessment returns preparationEvidenceSha256 . If a validation report directory exists, it also requires verified completed-report custody. An administrator can submit POST /api/tasks/ task /handoff/preparation with an X-Request-ID and the expectedAssessment , expectedRevision , and expectedEvidenceSha256 fields. GET on the same route returns the latest preparation, including its expiration and the original and candidate Agent identities. A preparation expires after 15 minutes on the control database clock. Until expiration or release, new commands and configuration edits for the task are blocked. The candidate reserves one task slot and one Worker slot. The first profile counts every task already assigned to the candidate as a potential Worker, including stopped tasks. Explicit and automatic task placement account for the reservation. A current administrator can immediately release it with POST /api/tasks/ task /handoff/preparation/release , an X-Request-ID , and expectedPreparation , then manage the original task again. Replaying the same accepted request with the same actor and input returns its recorded preparation even after release or expiration. This preparation keeps the original task owner and writer generation. Transfer execution requires verified source and failure evidence and separate journal and control-store fencing. To stage verified evidence during an active preparation, an administrator submits POST /api/tasks/ task /handoff/preparation/stage with X-Request-ID , expectedPreparation , expectedRevision and expectedEvidenceSha256 . The candidate checks the original archive digest and scope, verifies completed reports under their report locks and writes a sealed manifest with per-file SHA-256 values. The candidate then publishes the directory atomically under its private state path. An authenticated replay verifies the existing files without replacing them. A new Agent incarnation or an expired or released preparation requires a new review. The response reports counts and executionAuthorized: false . The candidate stages completed reports and closed receipts for custody only. The staged files have distinct names. The standard validation report reader refuses to open a staged directory. A candidate can hold up to 16 staging directories, including interrupted copies. Its live task registry, report paths and writer rights stay unchanged. For a new fixed-owner MySQL task with a PostgreSQL external journal and MySQL or PostgreSQL targets, set nodeId to the registered original Agent ID, set journal.managedWriter: true , and set journal.writerAssignment to a new UUID. Run java -jar rivomesh.jar init-writer task.yml with the journal credentials before creating the task on that Agent. Automatic placement and ordinary configuration changes to this writer binding are refused. Existing unassigned journals require their own migration. The standalone transfer-writer command refuses this journal even when the candidate configuration omits managedWriter . A verified preparation records the original assignment and a private successor assignment for this request. The response reports digests through writerActivation . When both stores use the same PostgreSQL JDBC URL and the control database role can lock the journal rows, checkedInControlTransaction confirms that the control transaction checked the same expired or released journal lease, capture cut, and acknowledged subscription positions. The task and writer placement stay with the original Agent during this check. For a managed task whose PostgreSQL control and journal share one database, the stage response can include offlineInventory with profile: CLOSED RECEIPTS ONLY . The stopped original Agent confirms that its private reports, failure records and raw captures are absent and that it has no previously adopted history. The Controller compares every closed receipt with the current authenticated command history. The candidate seals the exact receipt payload on its private volume and can recheck it there after the shared transfer archive is unavailable. Candidate state and the transfer archive must use disjoint paths. For disaster recovery, put the candidate volume in a separate storage failure domain. A previously sealed ordinary stage retains its unchanged readiness and needs a new preparation to certify complete inventory. This receipt certifies the bounded inventory; freezing a writer and changing ownership require separate execution steps. In the console, open Assess Agent handoff . After verifying the current evidence, choose Reserve task and Worker slots . You can view the same receipt and expiration from either Controller. During an active reservation, choose Stage reports and receipts to copy the verified report archive and closed receipts into private storage on the candidate. The console shows their counts after the candidate verifies them. Select Reverify staged reports and receipts to check the same files again. After reopening the panel from either Controller, Stage reports and receipts also verifies an existing staged copy for that reservation. Select Release reservation before sending a new command to the original task. After the control transaction commits ownership, open the handoff panel and select Refresh handoff status . Ownership committed means the candidate still needs to install the reviewed configuration. Candidate configuration installed records that the candidate saved the task in a stopped state. Evidence received adds the counts of verified reports and closed receipts received by the candidate. The panel binds the signed receipt to the candidate and the committed configuration. After the Worker is admitted, later lifecycle revisions leave the handoff receipt available. The same administrator needs grants for the task and both Agents. The verified same-store profile installs original reports and closed receipts after the internal transfer. The candidate can serve that history read-only from either Controller at the original cut. While it is stopped, HANDOFF PARKED and journal formats 15–18 block direct Worker launch and generic resume. Upgrade the Controllers and Agents that share this journal before running the new handoff profile. Older units refuse the new format. Worker start has its own approval after ownership transfer and SQL target fencing. Freeze the original writer An administrator can freeze the original writer while its Agent is healthy, the task is stopped and every SQL destination has acknowledged the same cut. This workflow requires an initial managed journal assignment, one PostgreSQL control and journal database, and a staged CLOSED RECEIPTS ONLY inventory. Retain offlineInventory.manifestSha256 from the staging response. Both Agent bindings and the task revision must still be current. Submit POST /api/tasks/ task /handoff/preparation/freeze-original with a new X-Request-ID and four JSON fields, expectedPreparation , expectedRevision , expectedEvidenceSha256 and expectedInventorySha256 . Give the inventory field the staged manifest digest. The candidate rechecks that exact private copy. The original Agent rechecks its stopped task, complete local receipts and current native cut. The shared PostgreSQL transaction advances the epoch, clears the original journal lease and records ORIGINAL FROZEN . Check the frozen epoch from either Controller in the preparation receipt. Ownership and destination data stay at the original cut. The freeze blocks ordinary START, configuration changes, release and ownership confirmation. To cancel a freeze, use POST /api/tasks/ task /handoff/preparation/cancel-freeze with the same four values and a different request ID. The original Agent must be healthy on the same private directory, including after a process restart. Cancellation rechecks its original inventory and native cut. Only a still-frozen record can be cancelled. The original assignment becomes available at a higher unclaimed journal epoch, and the task remains stopped until explicitly started. Repeating the same request reads the recorded phase. Cancellation requires restoring the original Agent if it is offline. Transfer a frozen task after losing the original Agent Use the frozen preparation and exact candidate enrollment recorded while the original Agent was healthy. The original node must report STALE after its exact registered lease expires on the database clock. Confirm the original Agent is unavailable. A live lease, a different original lease identity or an unavailable candidate blocks the transfer. For unplanned loss before a durable freeze, restore the original Agent and its private state. Open the frozen preparation in the handoff panel and refresh until the original Agent lease shows as expired. Review the freeze request and inventory digest, confirm that the original Agent is unavailable and choose Transfer frozen task ownership . For automation, the administrator who froze the task can submit POST /api/tasks/ task /handoff/preparation/commit-offline-owner from either Controller. Use a new X-Request-ID , the same four values used to freeze the task, and JSON boolean "confirmOriginalUnavailable": true . The request checks the freezing administrator’s current task and Agent permissions. The candidate rechecks its exact private sealed inventory and the native source and destination cut. The shared archive can be unavailable once the candidate copy is verified. A missing or modified candidate copy blocks transfer. The shared PostgreSQL transaction changes the task owner and assigns the previously frozen, unclaimed journal epoch to the candidate. Ownership then projects as a stopped task and the candidate adopts the closed receipts. Check the signed preparation from either Controller. Its offlineOwnerCommit identifies the freeze and approval requests. If the response is lost, reissue the identical request with the same administrator and request ID. After commit the original assignment is retired, including if its old directory and Agent later return. Keep the task stopped until the receipt reports EVIDENCE ADOPTED . Approve Fence SQL targets , wait for TARGETS FENCED and separately approve Start candidate Worker . The writable candidate resumes from the same cut. This workflow requires the initial managed MySQL-source journal assignment, a shared PostgreSQL control and journal database, PostgreSQL or MySQL targets, and the complete CLOSED RECEIPTS ONLY profile. Commit a reviewed owner change Stage and verify the evidence for a prepared same-store managed SQL handoff. The Commit ownership transfer action uses the exact staged receipt. The candidate checks its private files, writer configuration and authorization again before the control database commits ownership. The original Agent must have stopped at the reviewed cut. If original source or failure evidence still needs to be adopted, the transfer is refused. For automation, send POST /api/tasks/ id /handoff/preparation/commit-owner with X-Request-ID , expectedPreparation , expectedRevision and expectedEvidenceSha256 . Use the original prepared revision and digest. The Controller retrieves the private candidate configuration and preparation from signed records. An accepted transfer moves ownership to the candidate and parks the journal transactionally. The candidate then installs the task as stopped and receives the report history. If the Controller disconnects, read the preparation from either entry. Retry a bound operation with the same request ID. The preparation returns commitRequestId while a request is bound and after transfer. A fresh preparation is required when the reviewed cut, candidate binding or authorization changes before commit. Verify a handoff across separate journal and control databases A managed PostgreSQL journal in a separate database can verify the original stopped cut and stage reports and closed receipts under a reservation. The candidate must reach the journal, source and destinations as well as the control database. Restoring a disconnected journal route allows a fresh probe. An authenticated stage retry can verify an existing private copy when the shared archive is unavailable. The console shows why ownership commit is unavailable. The preparation returns checkedInControlTransaction: false and commitBlocker: HANDOFF MANAGED CONTROL CUT REQUIRED . Both Controller entries refuse ownership commit before binding the request. The original Agent and the journal and target checkpoints remain in place. Release the reservation to restart the original Agent from the same cut. Ownership activation across databases needs a separate durable protocol. Fence the parked SQL targets After the candidate has adopted the signed report and receipt history, an administrator can select Fence SQL targets in the handoff panel. For API approval, use POST /api/tasks/ id /handoff/preparation/fence-targets with X-Request-ID and the JSON fields expectedPreparation and expectedRevision . Use the preparation ID and the committed task revision displayed in the handoff panel. 202 acknowledges durable approval. Read GET /api/tasks/ id /handoff/preparation or refresh the handoff panel to follow FENCE PENDING and TARGETS FENCED . The first profile uses a MySQL source, one shared PostgreSQL control and journal database, and at most eight PostgreSQL or MySQL targets at a common original epoch. The candidate independently verifies its installed configuration, archived evidence, source log coverage, and original target checkpoints and snapshots. Each target transaction advances its writer epoch under its checkpoint row lock. Transaction receipts, snapshot IDs and source position remain at the reviewed cut. The journal stays parked and the Worker stays stopped. Keep the same request ID to read the receipt from either Controller. If the candidate or a database stops during execution, the approved request stays pending and the candidate resumes from the native target epochs when it returns. A different request cannot replace a current approval. If account authorization changes while fencing is pending, refresh and select Approve SQL fencing again . Use a fresh request ID when approving through the API. A changed cut or lost snapshot keeps the request pending. The handoff panel shows the latest verified blocker and its timestamp. The Agent log also records the HANDOFF TARGET FENCE diagnostic. Worker activation requires separate admission. Start the candidate Worker After Targets fenced , select Start candidate Worker . The API uses POST /api/tasks/ id /handoff/preparation/start-worker with a new X-Request-ID and the same expectedPreparation and expectedRevision as the fencing request. Retry an uncertain result with the same request ID and payload. Handoff state What to check --- --- START PENDING The approval is durable. The candidate checks the source cut and each native target checkpoint again. If a check fails, the Worker remains stopped. Refresh the handoff panel to see the latest blocker and when the candidate observed it. WORKER ADMITTED The shared PostgreSQL transaction opened the journal to the candidate assignment and recorded the approved request. The candidate still needs to save the local start intent. WORKER PROJECTED The candidate saved the start intent. Check the Worker state and capture lease in task details to confirm actual execution. Journal formats 19–22 mark the admitted assignment, preserve enabled recovery features and fence older runtimes. The candidate still acquires the normal exclusive lease and respects available Worker slots. It consumes the original source checkpoint and snapshot generation. Once the start intent is saved, use the ordinary task controls. Replaying the handoff approval preserves a later operator stop. Task and node grants govern access to original report history and closed receipts. New reports are stored in the candidate’s ordinary workspace. During the pending approval, a changed target receipt, unavailable source logs or a revoked administrator authorization leaves the task parked. Check the candidate log and restore the reviewed database state before retry. If authorization changes, an eligible administrator can refresh the handoff panel and select Approve Worker start again . The panel allocates a fresh request ID. API callers should use a fresh request ID and the existing preparation and committed revision. This profile covers the same PostgreSQL control/journal store and the same MySQL and PostgreSQL target profiles as the fencing step. Automatic host takeover and partition recovery have separate acceptance criteria. Admission and recovery PENDING is durable queueing. DISPATCHED saves the exact original local request/revision before invocation. ACCEPTED is local durable admission. SUCCEEDED/FAILED come from actual operation receipts. UNKNOWN requires reconciliation, not a success claim or reissue under a new revision. Startup restores receipt protection and validates local configuration against shared authority before scheduling. The latest startup fix scans all outstanding command pages, including undispatched STOP/PAUSE. Corresponding Workers cannot restore old RUNNING intent before local durable admission; older local operations may finish and stop commands receive priority retries. Rejection after authorization changes releases the block; uncertainty retains it. Focused tests and the application build pass; native business acceptance remains candidate-specific and does not retroactively change earlier evidence. TASK BUSY/OPERATION PENDING retain the original request. Outstanding receipts bypass ordinary 500-entry pruning. Cancellation has a parent and reserved capacity: cancel undispatched work atomically, reconcile uncertain delivery first, and perform actual cancellation after local admission. Success does not imply all targets rolled back. Offline STOP waits for the original owner. Restore its private directory or volume and the associated keys. In a combined deployment, Controller shutdown stops its local Workers. In a separate deployment, Agents have their own lifecycle. MySQL primary promotion has separate recovery procedures. Unexpected original Agent outage 1. Open the same task from either management entry. Execution node control lease shows the current lease in the shared control database. GET /api/tasks/ task returns ownerControlState alongside the existing ownerState , which also tracks whether the task observation is current. After the control lease expires, the Worker, run intent and capture lease are UNKNOWN . The assigned node and task revision retain their last committed values. A new process using the same node ID can acquire a control lease before it binds to the assigned directory. The task then shows registration in progress, with Worker and capture state still UNKNOWN . A different private directory is refused with AGENT DIRECTORY CHANGED . 2. Open Assess Agent handoff and check Original Agent control lease . A previous assessment becomes STALE . Start a new assessment to see ORIGINAL TASK STATE UNVERIFIED when the original Worker and its native cut are unverified. The probe refuses the assessment and the candidate gains no ownership or start authority from it. 3. To keep the task stopped when the original Agent returns, submit STOP from either entry and record its request ID. Restart the original Agent with its existing private directory, keys and node identity. Queueing STOP advances the task revision and preserves the active configuration version. Wait for the same request to reach SUCCEEDED and for both entries to show Worker STOPPED and capture lease UNCLAIMED or EXPIRED . Retain the source logs during the outage. Check the target positions before explicitly starting the original task. The control lease and journal capture lease each have their own native fence. The original Agent registers a new control generation when it reuses its directory, and the Worker acquires a new capture generation on start. Lease expiry alone is insufficient evidence of a drained Worker, complete private recovery evidence or the reviewed cut on both targets. The atomic handoff with control and journal in the same PostgreSQL database still requires current original Agent, source and target proofs and administrator approval. If the original Agent cannot return or the partition persists, keep the existing assignment while you recover that evidence. For an unreachable original Agent, the handoff receipt shows the last recorded drain cut, original report/receipt custody and whether the review still matches the current task. The offline panel is read-only. A complete independent archive and durable writer freeze are required to make such an outage eligible for future transfer. Asymmetric control-network partition For a managed writer with control and journal in the same PostgreSQL database, the Agent and its targets can remain reachable while the Agent loses its database path. Both management entries report the shared control lease as STALE after it expires. The Worker, run intent and capture lease are UNKNOWN while the entries lack a current signed observation. The Agent disarms starts for managed journal Workers when it loses control authority and terminates their local processes. It keeps the saved run intent and journal position. Once the link is restored, the same Agent must revalidate its signed directory, current lease generation and task configuration. It waits for former Worker processes to exit and loads durable STOP and PAUSE commands before allowing managed Workers to launch. This happens inside the original Agent process. To keep a task stopped while restoring the link, queue STOP through either Controller. Check the same request ID for SUCCEEDED and confirm the original task is stopped before starting it explicitly. Retain the source logs and verify both target receipts if a transaction was in flight. The candidate does not gain ownership from lease expiry. Separate control and journal stores, destination-specific cuts and approval without the original private evidence require their own validation. A SQL transaction in flight Each SQL destination has its own native transaction receipt and journal acknowledgement. During a control-path partition, the journal can already contain the source transaction while a destination still waits on a row lock. Compare the retained sequence and each destination receipt before deciding which delivery remains outstanding. PostgreSQL exposes blocking sessions through pg blocking pids . PostgreSQL lock inspection · PostgreSQL row locks The same-store fixture holds the PostgreSQL row lock until the former Worker has exited. The MySQL target already has a native commit and journal acknowledgement. Releasing the PostgreSQL lock while the original Agent is still partitioned leaves the former PostgreSQL transaction rolled back. After restoring the original Agent, wait for its queued STOP to succeed before explicitly starting it. The captured position stays at the recorded transaction and only the PostgreSQL delivery is replayed. The fixture checks the same transaction identity and counts one committed insert and one committed update in each target database log. A committed target with a missing journal acknowledgement During a partition a target's native checkpoint can be one transaction ahead of its journal acknowledgement. The target commits its business rows and native receipt together. Once the original Agent returns, the Worker compares the retained transaction's ID and projected hash with the target receipt. A matching receipt advances that destination's acknowledgement. The sibling target keeps its confirmed position. The accepted source position and both targets' prior business writes remain stable. The shared PostgreSQL control and journal fixture can interrupt the acknowledgement for either the PostgreSQL or the MySQL 8.4 target. The fixture first locks the chosen target’s business row, waits for the other target to commit and acknowledge the source transaction, then moves the lock to the chosen target’s journal acknowledgement row. The MySQL case verifies the real InnoDB record wait through Performance Schema. After the original Agent returns, confirm the queued STOP and explicitly start the task. The fixture checks the unchanged native receipt identities, the recovered acknowledgement and the commit history of both targets. MySQL native lock waits Managed PostgreSQL acknowledgements set a transaction-local idle timeout before acquiring journal row locks. The existing capture lease duration bounds the timeout and a shorter nonzero PostgreSQL session setting takes precedence. When a disconnected client has left an idle acknowledgement transaction, PostgreSQL rolls it back and releases its locks even while the Agent route remains down. PostgreSQL client connection defaults A permanently unavailable original Agent keeps the handoff blocked while its signed stopped state and private recovery evidence are missing. Administrator approval still requires the original directory binding, current evidence for the reviewed cut and the original and candidate node grants. An intact target receipt can settle a delivery acknowledgement while ownership remains assigned to the original Agent. Operations FAQ How do I distinguish accepted from executed? Inspect deliveryStatus, status, code and actual Worker/target checkpoints for the same request ID. HTTP 202 is not business commit evidence. Does refresh or another entry preserve login? Shared sessions restore identity subject to cookie domain, Secure, SameSite, expiry and revocation. Different domains require correct proxy/session configuration. Can A stop an offline owner? A durably queues STOP. It stays pending/unknown until the original owner supplies an actual receipt. Heartbeat expiry does not prove process termination. Can I edit owner fields, delete root tables or use an empty directory? No. Authenticated metadata, counts, private-directory identity, receipts and configuration projections reject missing/substituted authority. Does control-store failure fall back to local accounts? No. Management refuses control without shared authority. Existing data-process behavior follows its journal/lease/target protocol; management availability does not establish complete data-plane fencing. What belongs in backups? Coordinate the control database, every private directory, logs/reports/local journal, external journal if selected, and original keys. Restoring just a cursor or old control snapshot is insufficient; automated coordination and old-backup fault matrices remain open. What is already evidenced? Earlier candidates cover real PostgreSQL/MySQL control stores, two independent JVMs, HTTPS/shared login, A creating B-owned tasks and offline commands. Configuration fixtures also invoke real TaskService with fixture Workers. The startup fix and real cross-node business CDC are under additional acceptance. These do not establish all cluster, adapter or hardware profiles. Why is no persistent preview running? The user requested temporary fixtures only. They remove their own containers/volumes and leave unrelated resources untouched.

title: Apache Hive
text: Hive destination, recovery and FAQ 中文：Hive V3. Example: hive-v3.yml. Status The first independent native and actual mixed recovery profiles passed; the catalog retains an experimental label. CLI/Web V3 configuration, isolated JDBC, native HiveServer2 checks, ACID ORC history and latest-version views are implemented. Hive4.0.1/Java8 independent acceptance covered PK moves, keyless multiplicity, precision, lost-confirmation replay, case-folding, restart and older nonempty backup refusal. Actual MySQL8.4.13→PostgreSQL17.12+Hive passed snapshot/CDC, independent Hive outage and catch-up, worker SIGKILL resume, SQL constraint repair/retry, missing-view isolation and truthful pause fences. The final artifact/worktree-assets gate passed too; see evidence. This does not accept every Hive version, cluster or production capacity profile. The first fixture used the official apache/hive:4.0.1 ARM64 image, one HiveServer2, embedded Derby and a local warehouse. The Temurin 21 fixture also verifies a standalone Hive Metastore backed by PostgreSQL. HDFS/S3, Tez, Kerberos, TLS and clustered failover require separate acceptance. External PostgreSQL Metastore fixture Layout and consistency Hive is a versioned analytical destination, not the transactional JDBC sink or a Journal. Each source table has a managed ACID ORC history table in metadataSchema . A view with the source table name in the mapped database selects the latest internal identity/version, filters tombstones and exposes source columns only. A primary-key move writes an old-identity tombstone plus a new row. Identical keyless rows retain separate normalized identities. Retries may leave duplicate physical versions; the business view should expose one current row per identity. History row count is not source row count. Only Rivomesh writes this layout; do not edit history, ownership properties or tombstones. One source transaction can span multiple Hive statements/tables: cross-table source transaction visibility is not atomic . JDBC commit is not an atomic business-data/checkpoint boundary here. An unfinished snapshot or backlog is not a cutover barrier, and this layout cannot directly take over OLTP writes. Types Normalized source type Hive storage --- --- BOOLEAN / INT64 BOOLEAN / BIGINT UINT64 DECIMAL(20,0), bounded to unsigned 64-bit DECIMAL precision ≤38 DECIMAL(P,S), refusing overflow or rounding DECIMAL precision 38 STRING preserving digits and declared scale FLOAT32 / FLOAT64 FLOAT / DOUBLE; non-finite values refused STRING / JSON / DATE / TIME / DATETIME / TIMESTAMP STRING; not native JSON/temporal semantics BYTES / GEOMETRY base64 STRING preserving decoded bytes Generated columns retain evaluated values for expressions already supported by the source adapter; expressions are not recreated in Hive. Reassess comparison, ordering and query functions for the destination types, especially wide decimal strings. Full row images and explicit missing-vs-null checks remain required. First-profile names use ASCII letters/digits/underscore, cannot start with a digit, and are at most128 characters; mapped databases also follow common configuration length limits. Unsupported source names are not silently rewritten. rivomesh columns are reserved. UNIQUE, GSI and ordinary indexes Hive removed its old indexing feature from3.0; there is no equivalent ordinary B-tree conversion here. Official index documentation. Business secondary indexes are explicitly omitted. Review the differences and set acknowledgeIndexOmission: true ; initialization refuses secondary indexes without that acknowledgement. Source business UNIQUE is not enforced in Hive. GSI global routing, uniqueness, covering layout and performance are not retained. ACID/ORC/bucketing are not substitutes. Internal identity/version correctness is preserved. Convergence assumes an authoritative source, exclusive destination writes, complete catch-up and identity-preserving conversions; see index policy. Connection and deployment Require hive.txn.manager=org.apache.hadoop.hive.ql.lockmgr.DbTxnManager , hive.support.concurrency=true , hive.query.results.cache.enabled=false , and managed full-ACID ORC tables/views. Operate Metastore, warehouse, transaction cleanup and compaction; session flags alone are insufficient. Hive transactions. Only direct binary jdbc:hive2://host:port/database is accepted, with optional auth=noSasl none and ssl=true false . Discovery, HTTP, Kerberos, URL credentials, initialization scripts and arbitrary session options are refused. Credentials use separate fields/environment references. noSasl is a matching-server option, not the production security default. TLS is configurable but not accepted by native testing yet. queryTimeoutSeconds is1–1800 (default300). Binary socket timeout is bounded to5–120 seconds and internal connect retries are0. A timeout does not prove the statement was absent. Default SQL/response limits are4MiB/16MiB, at most10,000 returned rows; overflow fails rather than confirming truncated results. Events also obey maxMessageBytes . Use a dedicated writer with private metadata-table DDL/read/write and property/description/definition access, plus mapped view DDL/read. Minimum grants depend on the authorization plugin and remain to be verified. Readers should access business views only. check is read-only and cannot prove write permissions. Its hiveIndexPlans entries expose per-table index actions, required acknowledgement and columnStorage types; omission is never reported as an ordinary-index conversion. A pinned standalone Hive SDK runs in a private classloader without replacing core logging/Jackson/Guava. First use extracts and verifies about42MiB under a private java.io.tmpdir cache. Read-only Docker/K8s filesystems need a restricted writable temporary volume; do not share an untrusted cache. Confirmation and recovery Implementation writes versions, reads back actual identity/version/tombstone/values, writes and reads a target receipt, saves Journal transport progress, then advances the destination transaction checkpoint. Physical row count alone cannot confirm an uncertain write. Reconnect checks ownership, layout, view definition, resource properties and the latest receipt. Established missing objects are not recreated at old progress. Resource UUID is a Rivomesh Metastore property, not independently authenticated storage identity. Coordinate Metastore, warehouse and Journal backups. Arbitrary partial-table/file rollback, forged metadata or partial history loss are not claimed to be fully detected. The first independent native case passed server restart and refusal of an older nonempty Metastore+warehouse backup while Journal retains newer progress; see the exact release and scope in evidence. Connection failures retry by classification; deterministic structure/permission/data errors pause this destination. Resume retries original data, without changing GTIDs or silently skipping. Pause cannot establish that every in-flight Hive request has been cancelled. Journal ACK-based reclamation does not reclaim Hive history. Monitor history, tombstones, receipts and ACID delta files separately. Receipt compression, safe history GC, compaction soak and hardware sizing remain unfinished. FAQ Why append versions instead of ordinary UPDATE/DELETE? History, versions and tombstones support snapshot replay, uncertain requests, PK moves and keyless identity under one layout. Read the view rather than the physical table. Can Hive take over the application? This analytical layout has neither source cross-table atomicity nor enforced business UNIQUE. Takeover needs a separately designed data model, reconciliation, barrier and constraints. Does Hive block other destinations? Delivery threads are independent; other destinations can progress while Hive is unavailable. Unconfirmed data retains shared Journal space and eventually causes capture backpressure at quota. The first mixed profile passed; Journal exhaustion and the wider fault matrix remain unverified. Can an existing nonempty table be adopted? Arbitrary adoption/overwrite is not implemented. Ownership or shape mismatch is refused. Live DDL, nonempty adoption and repair require later workflows. How is the native case reproduced? After building, run bash tests/hive-materializer-run.sh . It operates only its own named volumes and stops the server before coordinated Metastore/warehouse backup/restore. Failed raw logs stay in target/ ; inspect actual scenario coverage rather than relying on a marker alone. The fixture uses HIVESERVER2 PID DIR on a dedicated ephemeral runtime mount to avoid a stale PID matching a new process after container restart. Metastore and warehouse remain persistent volumes. This fixture correction is not a production Hive HA implementation. Query cache and consistent reads The mixed fixture returned three detail rows but a cached COUNT0. A fresh session with only query-results cache disabled returned COUNT3 while stats optimization remained enabled. This observation does not establish the same problem for every Hive release/deployment. The first supported profile requires the server default and all reader sessions to use hive.query.results.cache.enabled=false ; the writer session must also disable it. Read-only preflight and write-time checks refuse enabled cache with HIVE QUERY CACHE DISABLED REQUIRED , without silently changing global settings. Disabling cache only on the writer cannot protect other readers. Do not re-enable it in application connections or manually add rows based on stale cached counts. Correct server/reader settings before check/resume; this does not require resetting data, task identity or checkpoints. The original cache-enabled mixed run was explicitly aborted and is not accepted complete recovery. The cache-disabled profile passed independent materialization/restart/older-backup refusal; the frozen-release complete mixed run passed too; see evidence. Java 21 outage and batch verification The ARM64 fixture uses MySQL 8.4.13 with PostgreSQL 17.12 and HiveServer2 4.0.1 destinations. When Hive stops, PostgreSQL continues and Hive keeps its journal acknowledgement and exact batch receipt. The fixture reads the original and later receipts directly from Hive and checks the same owner, resource UUID and warehouse location after HiveServer2 and Worker restart. Worker restart reuses the original snapshot. After a PostgreSQL constraint violation, replay to that subscription leaves the Hive receipt unchanged. Run RIVOMESH TEST PREBUILT=1 bash tests/hive-pipeline-run.sh after compiling the Java 21 JAR and test classes. The fixture restarts a single HiveServer2 with its embedded Derby Metastore and local warehouse volumes. Hive transactions · Verification record External PostgreSQL Metastore fixture Supply the PostgreSQL JDBC driver separately to run the Java 21 pipeline against HiveServer2 4.0.1, a standalone Hive Metastore and a dedicated PostgreSQL 17.12 catalog. The stock Hive schema tool initializes and validates the disposable catalog. The port probe waits for HiveServer2 to accept connections and Rivomesh then runs its normal JDBC checks. The completed native run passed seven checks. HiveServer2, Metastore and the catalog stopped together while the separate PostgreSQL business destination advanced. After restart, the PostgreSQL system identifier, Hive table ID, resource UUID, owner and warehouse location matched the original catalog. Worker SIGKILL resumed the original snapshot and four Hive batch receipts remained tied to the same resource. Replaying an independent PostgreSQL constraint error preserved the Hive receipts. Verification record HiveServer2 and Metastore share a local warehouse volume in this fixture. The restart retains the same PostgreSQL catalog and warehouse volumes. Distributed warehouse storage and automatic Metastore or PostgreSQL failover require their own tests. Apache Hive Docker setup The isolated Metastore's Hadoop core-site.xml grants its notification API to the hive identity from the HiveServer2 Compose hostname. Without that entry, HiveServer2 can fail at startup with get current notificationEventId authorization errors even when the PostgreSQL schema has passed validation. Hive 4.0.1 notification authorization

title: Implementation status

title: 金仓 Kingbase
text: Kingbase destination and FAQ 中文：金仓 V3. Example: kingbase-v3.yml. Scope and connection V3 configuration, CLI, explicit mappings, independent fan-out workers and the bilingual wizard accept product: KINGBASE . The first profile targets PG compatibility mode and remains EXPERIMENTAL . The first Java8/Kingbase V009R001C001B0025 PG/UTF8 native transaction and MySQL8.4.13+PostgreSQL17.12 mixed recovery profile passed; see evidence. Existing PostgreSQL results do not prove Kingbase compatibility. Other modes, RAC/distributed products, all versions and capacity remain pending. The pinned Java8 driver is cn.com.kingbase:kingbase8:9.0.1 , with com.kingbase8.Driver and jdbc:kingbase8:// , normally port54321. The vendor namespace coexists with PostgreSQL. Maven Central's vendor POM declares Apache-2.0; a complete distribution license/NOTICE review is still required. Every physical sink connection checks the actual product, version() , SHOW database mode , UTF8 encoding, empty-string preservation, case/trailing-space comparisons and writability before metadata access. It sets UTC, standard strings and synchronous commit=on . Only pg passes. The service never changes compatibility mode, global settings or database roles. Local synchronous commit still requires reliable server storage and suitable replication configuration; it does not prove multi-node failover durability. Have the DBA provision a UTF8 database, account and writable endpoint first. Each MySQL database explicitly maps to a schema within that Kingbase database. Rivomesh may create mapped schemas/tables/indexes and its metadata, but does not install the database or provision accounts. Provide metadata access and relevant schema/table/index creation plus business/checkpoint read/write privileges. A connection check does not prove all DDL/DML privileges. Use MYSQL PASSWORD / KINGBASE PASSWORD environment references or protected configuration. In the UI choose V3 and KingbaseES(PG), then explicit mappings. V2 does not enable this adapter. Linux, Docker, Helm and native Kubernetes use the same task document; deployment manifests do not deploy Kingbase. Data, indexes and recovery Business changes and the destination checkpoint commit in one local transaction, with metadata row locks and epoch fencing. An uncertain commit is resolved by rereading the destination checkpoint. Other targets acknowledge independently; this is not a distributed atomic commit. LOCAL Journal supports same-host recovery; cross-host worker takeover requires an already-supported external PostgreSQL/openGauss/MySQL journal. An unverified Kingbase journal backend is explicitly rejected. Keyless tables gain rivomesh row id to retain duplicate multiplicity. Supported generated expressions follow source-adapter support and their values become ordinary destination columns. UINT64 uses DECIMAL(20,0), decimals retain declared precision, JSON uses JSONB, binary uses BYTEA, microsecond times use TIMESTAMP(6), and signed/over24hour MySQL durations use INTERVAL. Procedures, triggers, foreign keys, partition layouts and arbitrary generated expressions are not automatically reproduced. DOWNGRADE BUSINESS turns business UNIQUE into ordinary indexes; primary/actual identity keys remain unique. Plain BTREE/simple business GSI can use the ordinary-index plan, losing global routing/global uniqueness. Expression, prefix, descending, fulltext and spatial methods require a separate plan. Downgrading assumes valid source constraints, complete ordered replication and exclusive synchronization writes. Reconcile and rebuild required constraints before takeover. Existing UNIQUE constraints are never silently dropped. Nonempty/incompatible targets require an adoption plan; the complete automated takeover workflow remains pending. Transient connection failures back off and reconnect; other sinks continue until journal backpressure applies. Deterministic SQL failures pause only that subscription. Repair the cause, then resume in the UI or with resume config/kingbase-v3.yml kingbase-business errorGeneration using the current status value and the same java -jar ... prefix. This retries the original transaction. Restart does not skip a pause. Missing tables/ownership/checkpoints refuse reuse of old progress; normal resume cannot repair lost data. TIME and native acceptance scope MySQL TIME is a signed duration, not a java.sql.Time/LocalTime wall clock. V3 snapshots and binlog events normalize it as [-]HH:MM:SS.ffffff . The pinned0.30.3 SDK uses duration overrides for ordinary/extended INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE row events; other fields retain its existing codecs. Native tests cover TIME2 precision0..6, negative fractions, over24hours and keyless identity. V2's accepted type range is unchanged. The real pipeline compares integer microseconds for positive/negative25hours, every fractional precision and negative1microsecond. Boundaries/malformed binary have unit coverage. Source reference SQL uses TIMESTAMPDIFF(MICROSECOND,...,ADDTIME(...)) ; this environment's integer TIME TO SEC result and default four-place SQL division are unsuitable microsecond oracles. This Kingbase version returns float8 from EXTRACT(EPOCH), so readback first casts to NUMERIC(20,6), then compares integer microseconds. A generic duration-text mapping does not imply native TIME acceptance for every other adapter. The same actual release also passed cross-schema business/checkpoint rollback, replay, alias ownership, old-epoch refusal, writable checks, PostgreSQL masquerade refusal, snapshot/CDC, target outage while PostgreSQL continues and subsequent catchup, worker SIGKILL preserving generation/snapshot, separate SQL constraint repair/retry on both targets, persistent SQL pause through restart, missing-table isolation and final transactional fences. Other versions/modes, primary/replica clusters/routing, TLS, old nonempty physical backup restore, power loss, soak and hardware capacity remain pending. Existing custom column collations and application takeover require separate assessment. FAQ - Other compatibility modes? They need separate semantics, catalog/type adaptation and native acceptance. Changing an existing instance's mode is not an automatic compatibility fix. - Product/mode mismatch? Check the actual endpoint and SHOW database mode . Do not disguise it as a PostgreSQL target to bypass validation. - SQL ASCII or other encoding? Older vendor images may initialize SQL ASCII. Have the DBA provision a UTF8 database or migrate encoding, then recheck; Rivomesh does not rewrite database encoding in place. - Read-only endpoint? A retryable connection error waits for a writable primary. Database operations perform promotion and endpoint routing; do not reset checkpoints. - String comparison rejected? Check case/trailing-space settings. This profile requires distinct comparisons and never changes global comparison rules. - Existing rows/constraints? Use an explicit adoption plan. Do not clear metadata or drop constraints to continue an old task. - Concurrent business writes? The downgrade profile requires exclusive synchronization writes. Bidirectional conflict handling and the takeover workbench remain pending. - Database installation/license? Supply a properly licensed vendor build for the architecture. Rivomesh does not distribute database binaries/licenses or bypass authorization. Test containers do not require privileged mode. Reproducible native fixture and references With a lawful compatible image available, run bash tests/kingbase-pipeline-run.sh ; override RIVOMESH KINGBASE IMAGE for the same-layout build. The test uses actual release-JAR workers with isolated MySQL8.4/PostgreSQL17/Kingbase services and removes only its own project/volumes. Initialization explicitly selects PG/UTF8 without case-insensitive initialization, running the native server as the image's kingbase user, without sudo/systemd/privileged. Different image layouts require fixture changes; replacing a version tag alone is not acceptance. Native Kingbase connection with an external Java 21 driver The external-vendor candidate on Temurin 21.0.13 loads the operator-provided kingbase8-9.0.1.jar and connects to KingbaseES V009R001C001B0025 ARM64 in PG/UTF8 mode. The test checks the driver's JAR origin and verifies that an invalid password returns SQLSTATE 28P01 . It uses synthetic row inputs through the packaged transactional sink to verify UINT64, DECIMAL(65,30), JSON and atomic rollback. After the same endpoint restarts, the sink keeps its snapshot and receipt, fences the old epoch and applies the next transaction once. Use a Java 21 JDK, the compatible local image and the external vendor JDBC candidate. - Official JDBC guide - Official Docker guide - Official parameter guide - Pinned JDBC POM

title: Managed repair
text: Managed data repair The first managed workflow passed real HTTP/Worker/database acceptance across LOCAL/H2 and external MySQL/PostgreSQL/openGauss journals,with MySQL8.4/PostgreSQL17 business destinations. Evidence. Full vendor,cluster,capacity and security acceptance remains incomplete. Workflow 1. Complete V3 row validation, keep the task paused and open its differing report. 2. Explicitly select differing destination/table pairs and create a plan. Initial profiles are MySQL/PostgreSQL,with a200table selection ceiling. Nothing is selected by default. 3. Open Review repair plan. Check destinations,tables,missing/extra/changed counts,creator and budgets. Explicitly check confirmation and execute. The browser sends the exact server-read plan hash rather than constructing business changes. 4. Inspect job results/target commit receipts. After failure/cancellation,review and retry the same plan;committed tables resolve from receipts without repeating DML. 5. Explicitly resume only after review and obtain a fresh validation when appropriate. Repair does not resume replication,change historical differences to MATCH or authorize cutover. Only authenticated ADMIN may create,review,execute or cancel. The server derives actor identity from authentication. Task/config revisions,request identity,plan hash,report seal and physical checkpoints constrain execution.
