Controller, Agent and Worker runtime verification Use one release package to start the actual processes on Temurin 21 and verify MySQL to PostgreSQL and MySQL snapshot and CDC. The report records each role’s JVM version, architecture and package hash.

title: Multi-database pipelines
text: multi-database, multi-target pipelines This manual covers multi-database, multi-target synchronization. formatVersion: 3 (V3 in some console labels) identifies the task configuration format, not a database version or development phase. Keep the default for new tasks; changing the number does not migrate an existing task. 中文：V3 运行手册. Updated 2026-11-15. V3 runs through the CLI and Web console. The wizard defaults to v3 and retains v2 single-database tasks. Formats/metadata are isolated; automatic v2 state migration is not implemented. Web wizard and recovery After signing in, create a task: 1. Keep V3 selected, enter the logical source, comma-separated databases, replication serverId and credentials. 2. Map each database explicitly. Add target instances with distinct IDs and their mappings. Select local or external transactional journals and quota. The plan masks every password, including JDBC URL passwords. Saving leaves the task stopped; check before starting. 3. Inspect snapshot/backlog and each subscriber's ACK. “Resume this target” uses its own error generation; global “Resume after repair” uses the pipeline generation. They are distinct operations. 4. Local stop only stops this worker. Shared pause blocks standby claims and attempts target-local fence confirmation. Unreachable targets remain unconfirmed, not falsely declared settled. Global resume does not clear independent target SQL pauses. Web local journals use the controller's private journals/ pipelineId directory. New YAML omits journal.path ; imports selecting an existing CLI journal path are rejected until a journal/target migration plan is prepared. Do not delete old state to bypass this check. External journals can be imported directly. Controller restart retains task/pause intent and the same managed journal/checkpoints. VIEWER/OPERATOR/ADMIN,local accounts/token rotation,exact task grants,configuration editing/history restore and durable audit are implemented. Managed validation and report-driven repair have explicit accepted profiles. Transactional PostgreSQL and MySQL have scoped profiles for commit confirmation, transaction skipping, gap verification, compensation and manual correction. Configure the corresponding gates in the first-release baseline. Plan business cutover separately. See failed transactions for phase diagnostics and recovery boundaries. DOM and real HTTP/database controls passed;visual and live Kubernetes UI acceptance remain pending. Configure and start Use pipeline-v3.yml. List databases within one logical MySQL topology in databases . Each target explicitly maps source databases to destination schemas/databases with mappings . Targets may subscribe to different subsets; every source database needs at least one target. Transactional products include GAUSS , POSTGRESQL , and MYSQL , plus first experimental KINGBASE, DM and OCEANBASE profiles within their documented acceptance boundaries; KAFKA / RABBITMQ / NATS JETSTREAM / REDIS STREAMS / PULSAR use the messaging protocol and map to message namespaces. Each target owns a delivery thread so stalled I/O cannot block others. MySQL journal/targets must be separate physical instances from the source: server uuid checks reject feedback loops even through address aliases. check reads source objects and target connections without initializing state or creating tables. It does not establish all DDL/snapshot privileges. Running creates metadata and missing business tables. Existing tables must match, be empty, and have no foreign keys/triggers. Nonempty targets require a migration plan and are blocked without clearing data. The synchronizer exclusively writes subscribed business tables. Sources require GTID, ROW/FULL, replica-update logging, no transaction compression/partial JSON images, and no anonymous/tagged GTIDs. Snapshots additionally need permission for short FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK : establish the InnoDB read view, verify schema, record GTIDs and open the cursor before releasing the lock. Reading a large table retains its MVCC view and metadata lock; monitor source undo history and waiting DDL. Snapshot, CDC and recovery The UI separates source snapshot preparation from destination delivery. TARGET SNAPSHOT remains active until every subscription has confirmed the current source manifests. “Source snapshot rows” counts source artifacts; each target has its own confirmed-table count. A message confirmation is still not consumer completion. Each completed target table is acknowledged immediately, allowing its source parts to be reclaimed once all targets confirm that table. Source commits and capture positions are journaled atomically. Each table has an independent snapshot baseline and checksummed parts. Completed artifacts are reusable; an incomplete source snapshot restarts the whole table because a lost MVCC read view cannot resume. Target part checkpoints resume committed parts without duplicates. Keyless tables preserve every duplicate occurrence using rivomesh row id ; source columns conflicting with this name are rejected. Complete before images match one occurrence. Identity mutations and normalized events commit once in source order, and every target reuses that result. Slow replay never mutates identities again. JSON comparison ignores object order/numeric scale while preserving SQL NULL versus JSON null. Stored generated values come from the log. Whitelisted deterministic virtual expressions use versioned expressions and historical logged inputs, never current source rows. Destination columns are ordinary materialized columns. Evaluation pins the snapshot SQL mode and UTC. Unlisted functions, missing base images, or historical schema mismatches stop progress. This does not promise arbitrary client-session SQL-mode query semantics. Plan native generated columns and application writes before takeover. Each transactional target commits data and its checkpoint together under an epoch fence. Targets acknowledge independently; one paused target does not stop others. An uncertain commit is resolved by checking the destination transaction ID/content hash before acknowledging the journal. Multiple targets are not one distributed atomic transaction. Table snapshots can have different baselines; cross-table takeover requires a common catch-up point. The MySQL+transactional-SQL common-cut Java service passed initial native acceptance; see Reconciliation foundation. See managed validation and reviewed repair for the initial SQL profiles. Business cutover remains open. Retention follows the slowest subscriber, including paused ones. Snapshot parts are reclaimed only after every target confirms completion; manifests, baselines and keyless identities remain. Losing target metadata after artifact reclamation requires a rebuild plan. maxBytes covers logical event, normalized event, snapshot and identity payloads, including unconsumed normalization workspace reservations. Database indexes, WAL, metadata and free pages need additional capacity; reclamation does not immediately shrink physical files. Large-catalog pagination, physical headroom alerts, receipt compaction and oversized-transaction staging remain unfinished. Logical quotas are not total disk quotas. An open transaction gap or a prepared skip pins the exact raw and normalized transaction in the journal. Other fully acknowledged transactions can still be reclaimed. A verified gap releases its pin after the common-cut receipt is checked. If the pinned evidence fills the journal, capture waits without advancing the source position and the Worker records JOURNAL BACKPRESSURE . If capture needs more space to reach a fresh common cut, increase logical capacity before verifying the gap. Verification of an existing valid paused cut does not add event payload to the journal. Keep the original evidence and journal together during recovery. Raw capture reserves its normalization copy, keyless row IDs and potential identity additions. Normalization consumes that reservation atomically, preventing raw backlog from using the space needed to drain itself. When a slow destination exhausts available capacity, capture waits without advancing unpersisted GTIDs; deliveries, GC and lease heartbeats continue. Recovering consumers free space and capture resumes automatically. Local backpressure does not trigger the source-idle watchdog. Close/pause cancels the blocked receiver before waiting for the dump connection to finish. If one transaction and workspace exceed the entire quota, TRANSACTION EXCEEDS JOURNAL QUOTA preserves the old position. Insufficient snapshot/identity workspace, or old unreserved history that cannot be normalized after upgrade, raises JOURNAL WORKSPACE REQUIRES QUOTA PLAN . Source snapshots are currently all built before delivery; streaming reclamation across a large table, partial snapshot rebasing and oversized-transaction staging are unfinished. Expand capacity or use an explicit plan; never delete journal parts to make room. Quota is excluded from semantic identity: stop affected workers, change/reload configuration, then resume with the current global error generation. See configuration revisions for supported console changes. Use source.type: MYSQL in task configuration and the Web wizard. Identify the logical source cluster with source.clusterId and select its databases with databases . Set source.expectedVersion: "8.2.0" to require a patch version or "8.2" to accept that major and minor release. Preflight checks the candidate server version. Leaving the field empty enables detection. Journal choices LOCAL uses Java-8-compatible H2 2.2.224. path is a private directory, relative to the configuration file; it contains sensitive rows and receives mode 0700. Automatic server mode binds to loopback by default so the Worker and CLI can share the same local journal without depending on the host’s external name resolution. It is not a cross-host database service. Preserve the whole directory/volume; do not copy a live .mv.db alone. Use EXTERNAL for cross-host takeover; shared-filesystem H2 has not been accepted as a cluster journal. EXTERNAL supports PostgreSQL, openGauss or a separate MySQL instance. Workers share journal instance/namespace/pipelineId and target configuration, with distinct nodeIds. Database-clock leases and epochs fence ownership. MySQL storage must use InnoDB and retain acknowledged commits across restart. External HA systems promote/fence database nodes; Rivomesh does not promote them. V3 worker-crash recovery, MySQL 8.4 async promotion and MGR election during snapshot passed; other versions/soak matrices still need acceptance. V2 results do not prove all V3 variants. MySQL 8.2.0 source regression Run tests/matrix.sh --v3 8.2.0 for the V3 standalone, GTID async and single-primary group replication suites. The tests use Docker Compose, the mysql:8.2.0 source image and reports under target/matrix-v3/8.2.0/ . The source uses GTID, ROW binlog and FULL row images. In the async suite, the fixture promotes a caught-up replica and Rivomesh validates the required history before resuming from the original position. MySQL 8.4 binlog profile MySQL 8.4 uses untagged GTIDs, ROW binlogs and FULL row images. Preflight refuses anonymous-capable mode, tagged history, partial JSON and transaction compression. Capture stops before the failing transaction if it sees partial JSON or a compressed event. Review the retained logs and available source history before resuming or building a new baseline. Use tests/mysql84-profile-run.sh to reproduce the admission and live refusal checks. The fixture writes a tagged test transaction in its disposable database and cleans up afterward. MySQL GTID format · Binary log options Automatic continuation after MySQL 8.4 primary failure Set source.topology: ASYNC and supply the primary and replica as candidate source.nodes within one GTID replication topology. The external database HA service fences the failed primary and promotes a caught-up replica. Rivomesh verifies the promoted source's available GTID history and reconnects from the saved position. If the replica is still read-only or replication has an I/O error, investigate the topology while retaining the journal and target checkpoints. The Java 21 native profile used MySQL 8.4.13 asynchronous GTID replication, an external PostgreSQL journal, two management entries and PostgreSQL and MySQL destinations. After the old primary was killed, both entries showed the capture interruption and the two target checkpoints held. External promotion returned a writable source. Rivomesh delivered the new primary's GTID to both destinations with the original configuration revision, journal generation and snapshot IDs. Reproduce with python3 tests/global-control-pipeline.py --separate-execution --mysql-async-failover --source-expected-version 8.4.13 --artifact release jar --output target/mysql-async-proof . Verification archive A separate Temurin 21 test runs the same packaged JAR with MySQL 5.7.44, 8.0.46, 8.2.0 and 8.4.13, each with a PostgreSQL 17.12 destination and journal. It terminates the original Worker, induces a real replica SQL-thread error 1032, verifies that the unhealthy replica is refused, restores replication and shuts down the original primary. After external promotion it verifies the original snapshot ID and new target rows. Purging an uncaptured binlog range keeps the prior journal checkpoint and pauses capture. To reproduce after building the release JAR and test classes, run RIVOMESH TEST PREBUILT=1 SYNC V3 HA POSTGRES ONLY=1 SYNC MYSQL IMAGE=mysql:8.2.0 bash tests/v3-ha-run.sh . For 5.7 add SYNC MYSQL57=1 SYNC MYSQL57 IMAGE=mysql:5.7 . MySQL 8.4 single-primary Group Replication recovery Set source.topology: GROUP REPLICATION and list the members of one single-primary group in source.nodes . MySQL elects the writable member. Rivomesh checks that the candidate is online and writable and retains the required GTID history. Protect a restarted former primary with MySQL super-read-only until it rejoins. Group Replication requires a primary key or equivalent unique key on replicated tables. Single-primary mode · Group Replication requirements The Java 21 native test uses MySQL 8.4.13, an external PostgreSQL journal and a PostgreSQL 17.12 destination. It kills the primary, records a different server UUID and verifies that the same Worker delivers both subsequent transactions. The journal generation, two snapshot IDs and full destination rows agree. The former primary restarts read-only with a missing group GTID. MySQL refuses writes. The released JDBC driver reaches the old member at the unchanged endpoint and verifies its UUID and read-only flags before source preflight returns SOURCE NO PRIMARY . After it catches up as a secondary, capture continues on the elected primary. Reproduce with a Java 21 JDK, Docker Compose and local mysql:8.4 and postgres:17 images. A second Temurin 21 profile runs the same release JAR on MySQL 5.7.44, 8.0.46, 8.2.0 and 8.4.13. It shuts down the original primary while a snapshot is still being built. After MySQL elects a replacement, Rivomesh rebuilds the unfinished snapshot and both SQL destinations receive the pre-election update and subsequent insert, delete and update. Both journal ACKs reach the captured sequence. Reproduce with the prebuilt JAR and compiled tests using RIVOMESH TEST PREBUILT=1 SYNC V3 GROUP SQL TARGETS=1 SYNC MYSQL IMAGE=mysql:8.2.0 bash tests/v3-group-run.sh . For MySQL 5.7 add SYNC MYSQL57=1 SYNC MYSQL57 IMAGE=mysql:5.7 . Version-specific evidence Verified TLS for MySQL capture and delivery Configure source.sslMode: VERIFY IDENTITY for the binlog channel and include sslMode=VERIFY IDENTITY in source.jdbcOptions for discovery and snapshots. Each MySQL target has its own JDBC URL and TLS options. Install the CA roots in the execution JDK trust store available to the Agent and its Worker JVMs. Use the certificate's DNS names in the source candidates and target URLs. The verified binlog modes negotiate through the JDK and can connect to a TLS 1.3-only MySQL endpoint. Connector/J TLS properties On MySQL 8.4.13, the real binlog and target JDBC sessions reported TLS 1.3. Preflight rejected a wrong source DNS name. After process termination the Worker reused the original GTID and snapshot, and the targets matched exactly. Reproduce with python3 tests/mysql-tls-run.py --java-home Temurin 21 directory --artifact release jar --output target/mysql-tls-proof . Verification archive Standalone writer transfer with a PostgreSQL journal For a new standalone MySQL pipeline, set journal.mode: EXTERNAL , journal.product: POSTGRESQL and journal.writerAssignment to a fresh UUID. Use up to eight PostgreSQL/MySQL targets and 256 source tables. Keep the journal, target metadata and source logs accessible on both Workers, and reserve an independent private directory for any report files you generate separately. init-writer creates the initial placement of a new pipeline. An enrolled Worker opens the existing journal on restart. A missing journal or placement requires restoring the original state. The command rejects enrollment on a previously created ordinary journal. Earlier application builds refuse the enrolled journal format. Wait for the original snapshot and every target acknowledgment to catch up. Stop the original Worker cleanly, or wait for its database-clock lease to expire after a failure. Use status original.yml to obtain generation , epoch and writerPlacement.assignment . Create a private candidate configuration with the same pipeline and destination settings, a different nodeId if changing hosts, and a fresh journal.writerAssignment . Ensure the candidate can read the original source logs and native target metadata. The command verifies GTID history, the original snapshot IDs and target receipts before changing the placement. A live lease, incomplete snapshot, lagging/paused targets, or an unresolved skip intent blocks transfer. If confirmation is lost, repeat the exact original command to recover its durable receipt. A successful transfer keeps the capture position and target acknowledgments. The candidate claims a newer lease. The former configuration cannot claim or renew a lease, and a retired assignment UUID cannot be reused. Use a new UUID for any later transfer, including a move back to the original host. A paused or incomplete job must recover on its currently assigned Worker first. The cluster console manages Agent assignments separately. This CLI workflow covers the standalone Worker, the existing shared journal and transactional targets. It leaves report files and Agent ownership in their original locations. Troubleshooting and FAQ - SQL errors: only that subscriber pauses with an error generation. Repair privileges/schema/data, then resume the original transaction using the current generation from status . Resume never skips data or edits GTIDs. - Connection loss/deadlocks: transient errors retry; local destination fencing blocks stale owners. Source reconnect validates candidate GTIDs and snapshot dependencies. Missing logs/multiple writers block or wait without rewinding progress. - Journal quota: CDC backlog uses the backpressure/recovery path above; snapshots or indivisible oversized commits need capacity/error-generation plans. Budget snapshot/identity copies, normalization reservation and the backlog window. Backpressure cannot reconstruct permanently lost storage or source binlogs purged before they were read. - Live DDL: currently blocks safely, including potentially unrelated-database SQL that could reference selected objects. Historical DDL evolution and explicit skip plans are unfinished. - UNIQUE(email): DOWNGRADE BUSINESS creates an ordinary secondary index. Source constraints, exclusive sync writes and transactional/idempotent checkpoints jointly preserve source uniqueness. Validate and restore constraints before application writes. Primary, identity and internal keys are never downgraded. - GSI: business GSI model entries can become ordinary indexes, losing global routing/uniqueness. Identity GSIs require a distribution plan. Existing GSIs/unique constraints are never blindly dropped. Commercial distributed GaussDB is not hardware-validated. - Expression/prefix/descending/special indexes: require a separate plan; the target pauses instead of silently omitting them. Unsupported indexes block before creating a missing table. - Types: common integers/unsigned, decimal/floating point, text/binary, YEAR, DATE/DATETIME/TIMESTAMP and JSON are covered. V3 now implements signed microsecond MySQL TIME durations with matching JDBC snapshot and TIME/TIME2 row-event text. Relational targets use INTERVAL/MySQL TIME(6); analytical/event targets retain duration text. See the Kingbase guide and DM guide for first native acceptance scope. BIT, ENUM/SET, spatial/zero dates, non-InnoDB and other objects need extension/testing. - V2 migration: continue the old configuration to retain v2 checkpoints. Adding formatVersion: 3 cannot take over a populated old target. Explicit data/state migration planning remains necessary. Replace 1 with the relevant subscriber or pipeline error generation. Stale requests are rejected. Permanent source errors persist as ERROR and block standby claims; pause reports each fence confirmation. RBAC/local accounts/configuration editing/audit are implemented. See implementation status for scoped recovery. LOCAL connection lifetime and controller memory The controller retains a stable connection to each opened LOCAL journal, including paused/stopped tasks, until configuration replacement or controller shutdown. On restart it opens existing files; inspecting a never-started task does not create its journal. Same-host CLI/certificate/repair operations therefore share a stable H2 automatic-server endpoint. Each opened journal has a 4 MiB page-cache setting plus schema/index metadata and connection-thread overhead. Worker heaps, control-store connections and IAM/audit state consume additional memory. Docker/Linux/Helm controller defaults now use a 512 MiB maximum heap; Helm exposes controllerHeapMiB . Size by initialized LOCAL journal count, schema volume and measured heap use; maxTasks limits task count. External transactional journals are available for larger installations. Optional protocol5 adds administrator evidence creation,raw/normalized pages and typed image review. See review operations for activation/upgrade and deployment profiles. Default legacy profiles do not upgrade automatically. See implementation status for scoped recovery.

title: Platform design
text: Rivomesh complete product and technical design Updated: 2026-11-15. 中文：完整方案. See requirements for decisions and status. This is the full design, not a claim that every feature is complete. V3 now supports multiple explicitly mapped databases within one logical MySQL source, fan-out, multiple configurations with isolated workers, optional durable journals and Web management. The v2 single-database/single-target mode remains compatible. See implementation status and validation for each adapter's accepted scope, and the console manual for operations. Remaining capabilities follow the phases below. 1. Product and scope Rivomesh serves enterprise/government database migration, continuous replication, data distribution, validation, and cutover orchestration. A bilingual Web workbench guides ordinary installations; configuration files, APIs, and CLI use the same model for experts. Dimension Scope --- --- Current delivery source MySQL, including existing 8.0/8.4 coverage; standalone, GTID replication, single-primary MGR Future sources PostgreSQL and Oracle; design Source SPI and neutral event/position models now, without claiming available connectors Relational targets MySQL, PostgreSQL, openGauss, distributed GaussDB, DM, Kingbase, OceanBase, GBase; profile product/version/mode/engine separately Analytics/warehouse targets ClickHouse, Apache Doris, Apache Hive; classify GBase analytical/transactional variants by actual capabilities Current delivery message targets Kafka, Pulsar, RabbitMQ, RocketMQ, ActiveMQ (separate Classic/Artemis profiles), Redis Streams, NATS JetStream Deployment Linux manual, Docker, Kubernetes Helm, native Kubernetes manifests Storage Local durable journal, eligible target-hosted journal, independent shared journal Broad version coverage means an expanding compatibility matrix and capability detection, not unconditional support for every historical release/fork/combination. Mark features verified/experimental/unverified/unsupported and identify actual products, versions, modes, drivers, hardware, and recovery boundaries. JDBC connectivity is insufficient acceptance evidence. 2. Multiple tasks and targets Each independent configuration defines one logical source, object selection, multiple targets, mappings, storage, and resource policy. Different configurations may connect to independent MySQL clusters. Support standalone task processes and a console managing isolated workers. Never implicitly merge sources into one transaction or destination table. Tasks, subscriptions, tables, targets, configuration revisions, and stream generations have independent identities. Candidate endpoints belong to one topology; database mappings are explicit. Preflight detects overlapping destination writers, replication loops, changed source identity, and fingerprint conflicts. New targets establish their own baselines. Isolate rate, connection/thread, memory, and disk quotas per task. Independent configurations capture separately by default. Explicit capture sharing may follow after validating privileges, filters, retention, source identity, and recovery dependencies, not merely matching hosts. Preserve cross-database transaction atomicity only within a target scope supporting it; no cross-target global XA. 3. Modules and contracts - Source SPI: discover capabilities/objects, create consistent baselines, capture transactions/DDL, encode/restore positions, validate failover, acknowledge upstream. GTID is not a universal source abstraction. - Journal SPI: persist complete transactions/large-transaction fragments, publish atomically, checksum, recover, enforce quotas, and reclaim. Advance safe capture only after durable completion. - Sink SPI: capability/object planning, write/publish, resolve uncertain commits, idempotency/versioning, DDL recovery, visibility. Model transactional writes, versioned materialization, batch publication, and messaging explicitly rather than assuming JDBC transactions everywhere. - Control/Worker: leases/fencing, isolation, configuration revisions, resource scheduling, and recoverable operation logs. Console outages must not destroy deployed worker checkpoints. - Validation/Cutover: baselines/barriers, differences, restored constraints, write ownership, and audit. Event envelopes carry logical sourceId, streamGeneration, transaction identity/ordinal, schemaVersion, table identity, operation, before/after, field-presence bitmap, snapshot/DDL/transaction boundaries, source position, and origin. IDs remain stable across retries and physical source failover; new baselines/lineages use new generations. Timestamps are observational, not ordering authorities. Positions are versioned typed payloads: MySQL GTID/dependencies, PostgreSQL LSN/slot/database/instance lineage, Oracle SCN/transaction/redo context, interpreted by their adapters. Do not compare them lexically or retain only the maximum observed SCN/LSN while losing open long transactions. Snapshot fragments also require stable IDs, completeness markers, and checkpoints. Future PostgreSQL capture must handle exported snapshots, slot/WAL retention, REPLICA IDENTITY, unchanged TOAST fields, and failover-slot readiness. Oracle requires supplemental logging, redo/archive coverage, long transactions, RAC/CDB/PDB, LOBs, and lineage. Official references describe readiness requirements for PG slots and supplemental logging for Oracle CDC. PostgreSQL, Oracle CDC reference. Review driver/capture distribution terms separately; future connectors are not existing failback channels. 4. Target capabilities and consistency Target class Write design Boundary shown in UI --- --- --- MySQL/PG/domestic transactional databases Dialect-specific batches or native upsert; local apply checkpoint commits with business data Source-transaction atomicity within supported target scope; central control storage does not replace the local checkpoint ClickHouse Stable materialization identity, monotonic version, delete markers; engine-specific replacement/read views Background ReplacingMergeTree merges do not guarantee deduplicated raw reads; validated FINAL/view contracts, no assumed cross-table transaction Doris Validated Unique Key/Merge-on-Write, sequence, deletes, Stream Load batch protocol Detect actual single/multi-table commit scope; resolve labels/txn state, timeouts, and retention windows per version Hive ACID capability mode or immutable file/partition/snapshot publication Ordinary tables are not row-oriented replicas; profile update/delete, visibility, transactions, and compaction Messaging Publish change events and transaction/snapshot boundaries with stable IDs Publisher confirmation is not downstream business completion; at-least-once by default, consumers must be idempotent ClickHouse replacement uses ORDER BY; mutable attributes or unstable partitioning cannot define row identity. Keep routing stable and coordinate old-version/tombstone cleanup with the oldest replayable position. Official engine guide. Doris Unique Key is a row-materialization model, distinct from a relaxable source business secondary UNIQUE. Do not mechanically replace it with Duplicate Key. Resolve lost acknowledgments against actual commit state; expired labels are not permanent deduplication evidence. Sequence columns, load transactions. These references do not guarantee every older version. Hive publication records batches, file manifests/digests, partitions, schemas, and metadata commit state. Readers must not see temporary files; object storage cannot be assumed to provide atomic rename. Recovery reconciles files/catalog to prevent duplicates, partial batches, and orphans. ACID mode instead uses validated transaction APIs/configuration and compaction. Hive Transactions. Analytical targets default to data-service/warehouse output, not unverified OLTP application takeover destinations. Expose captured (durably collected), delivered (accepted), applied/materialized, visible under the declared read contract, and validated at a barrier as supported. A single success indicator must not hide these differences. 5. No-PK tables, JSON, generated columns All three are first-release requirements needing development; current code rejects them. Removing validation does not implement support. Identity class Planned strategy --- --- Primary key Stable keyed scan/lookup, including key changes No PK but a reliable all-NOT-NULL unique candidate Validate semantics, use it as identity, handle changes; do not casually relax this identity constraint No unique key; identical duplicate rows allowed Consistent baseline, multiset semantics, durable technical identities/counts, exact before-image matching; each change modifies one occurrence A target auto-ID, unique whole-row hash, or online OFFSET cursor cannot solve keyless identity. Hashes only accelerate candidates; compare full typed values and preserve multiplicity. Never delete every equal row for one logged deletion. Added technical columns require explicit mappings/views and dependency checks; they cannot be claimed invisible to SELECT . Keyless snapshotting needs a replayable consistent artifact coordinated with the log baseline. Persist fragments/manifests before loading and replaying later transactions; deduplicate imports by fragment/transaction identity. If a source MVCC snapshot disappears with its connection, a row number cannot restore it. Resume completed artifacts or rebuild that table at a provable new baseline without resetting unrelated completed subscriptions. The same applies to failover during an unfinished keyless snapshot. Explain required coordination privileges, possible short locks/rescans, and disk costs; do not promise arbitrary keyless tables lock-free exact row-cursor recovery. MySQL row-search behavior is a design reference, not reused storage internals. JSON: decode MySQL binary JSON correctly, preserving numeric precision, SQL NULL versus JSON null, array ordering, and characters. Map to native JSON or text/LOB with declared query differences. Compare using documented semantic normalization rather than object-key ordering/whitespace. Initially require full JSON logging and retain empty binlog row value options unless partial-patch/historical-base recovery is implemented. MySQL JSON replication. Generated columns: distinguish STORED/VIRTUAL, actual logged presence/values, dependencies, and schema versions. Choose proven equivalent target expressions or ordinary-column materialization. Missing logged values require evaluation from historical inputs, never a later SELECT of the source's current row. Translation/evaluation covers SQL mode, collation, time zones, precision, and JSON functions; unsupported expressions produce precise blockers/alternatives, never silent NULLs. Do not INSERT explicit values into native target generated columns. Record takeover differences between materialized ordinary columns and native generation. MySQL generated columns. 6. DDL, existing targets, constraints Discover/version table definitions, indexes, expressions, and dependencies. Ordered DDL needs schema barriers and recoverable operation logs. Classify transformations as automatic, planned migration, or blocked; never forward arbitrary source SQL. Reconcile catalogs after nontransactional DDL, restarts, and uncertain responses. Existing-target paths: compatible empty tables; nonempty staging/shadow comparison/publication; explicit merge policies using reliable keys; or incremental onboarding with proven matching data and log position. Entering a GTID without a verified baseline is insufficient. Keyless merges require multiset rules, not guessed upserts. Report extra/conflicting rows and trigger/FK side effects before changing anything; no automatic clearing. Relax Gauss business secondary UNIQUE to ordinary indexes; permit capability-driven relaxation for incompatible constraints on other targets, retaining original definitions. Preserve PK/candidate identity, internal deduplication, and required analytical materialization keys. Report missing equivalents instead of inventing indexes. See index policy for GSI and constraint restoration. 7. Three journal deployment modes Mode Use Availability/recovery limits --- --- --- LOCAL Single-host/Docker without extra services; persistent directory/PVC Process recovery; cross-node takeover requires original logs, authoritative owner verification, and old-writer fencing, otherwise automatic HA is disabled TARGET Reuse a validated transactional target's metadata schema No independent store, but its outage may block capture; not the default for ClickHouse/Hive/MQ-only tasks EXTERNAL Independent HA journal/state adapter and worker takeover Better isolation, but validate backend/acknowledgment/reclamation; arbitrary shared folders/object stores are not inherently safe journals Durable acknowledgment, checksums, transaction completion, stream sequence, and ownership form one protocol. Spill large transactions to durable fragments without marking partial transactions captured. Transactional sinks must not split an atomic source transaction just to save memory. Diagnose limits or use an explicitly supported mode rather than OOM and lose recovery context. Reclaim according to the slowest active subscription and baseline dependencies. Alert/backpressure near quotas and show retention headroom. Abandoning a target's history requires an explicit resnapshot plan. A message broker as sink and as internal journal are different roles; a sink connector does not automatically implement its journal backend. 8. Seven messaging families Target Adapter concerns --- --- Kafka Partitioning, durable acknowledgments, producer idempotence/transactions, transactional-ID fencing, schema/compression; restart/external-checkpoint recovery still required Pulsar Partition/routing, stable producer identity/sequence, persistent topics, deduplication windows/transactions RabbitMQ Durable queues/messages, publisher confirms, mandatory/returns, uncertain resend after reconnect, bindings RocketMQ Versioned normal/FIFO support, routing keys, acknowledgment/retry; transactional messages do not automatically couple source-log commits ActiveMQ Classic / Artemis Separate protocol/driver profiles, persistent messages, session/send acknowledgments, transactions/reconnect; Artemis features do not imply Classic parity Redis Streams XADD, persistence/replication, streams/groups and retention; generated stream IDs do not replace eventId NATS JetStream Durable streams, publish acknowledgment, subjects/consumers, deduplication IDs/windows, quotas; not ephemeral Core NATS The common contract is at-least-once publication with stable eventId and consumer idempotency by event ID/row version. Start with JSON envelopes and allow Avro/Protobuf/schema-registry plugins without a mandatory registry. Preserve type information and notify versioned schema/DDL changes. Choose per-table/key ordering or whole-transaction single-partition routing. Partitions, redelivery, and concurrent consumers do not imply global order. Large messages/transactions require transaction IDs, fragment ordinals, completion counts/markers, and checksums; atomic consumer application waits for complete assembly. Boundary records identify filtering scope so consumers do not wait for excluded rows. Kafka/Pulsar broker transactions, deduplication windows, or idempotent producers do not automatically provide end-to-end exactly-once across source, broker, and arbitrary consumer databases. RabbitMQ explicitly documents duplicates after lost confirmations. RabbitMQ reliability. Every adapter needs uncertain-commit recovery tests. Redis Streams and JetStream have their own retention, acknowledgment, persistence, and deduplication configurations; API availability is not durable-delivery validation. Redis Streams, JetStream. Validate ActiveMQ variants separately: Classic transactions, Artemis deduplication. Never skip bad messages by default. Missing routes, oversized messages, and serialization failures pause publication with guided UI repair. Any future quarantine-and-continue mode must retain replayable events and explicitly downgrade transaction/completeness guarantees. Broker retention/consumer completion are separate monitoring layers after publication; publish progress must not claim every subscriber has processed an event. 9. Fault model Cover source promotion/replication I/O and SQL errors, split writers, process/node failure, target outages/SQL errors, uncertain commits, disk full/corruption, interrupted DDL, lost MQ acknowledgments, duplicates/reordering, partial analytical batches, upgrades, and backup rollback. Retry transient errors with backoff; pause affected subscriptions for deterministic issues. Restarts/standby activation never bypass pause. UI exposes cause, scope, last safe positions, backlog, and recommended actions, then retries the original unit after repair. Do not offer casual position editing/transaction skipping. External database HA owns promotion/old-primary isolation; CDC cannot reconstruct permanently lost source data. 10. Graphical workbench Wizard: scenario → connections/tests → objects/privileges → compatibility/constraints/storage/sizing → explicit mapping → execution plan → run/diagnose → barrier validation → cutover/handover. Pages include overview, connections/drivers, tasks/subscriptions, object differences, journal/capacity, indexes/DDL, validation, incident center, cutover plans, deployment diagnostics, and audit. Explain causes/next steps in plain language; experts can expand SQLState/vendor codes and sanitized diagnostics. Stable codes have equivalent Chinese/English explanations. Pause/resume, retry, mapping/concurrency changes, object repair, table rebuild, validation, and cutover use authorized APIs with request IDs, expected configuration versions, idempotency, background-operation state, and audit. Browsers never edit metadata tables directly. Destructive plans show affected objects/recovery points without default data deletion. CLI/files use the same service contract for automation/offline operation. Separate viewer, operator, migration, and credential roles. Never put passwords in logs/plain exports. Provide offline help, diagnostic bundles, metrics/alerts; telemetry upload is not a runtime requirement. UI recovery does not replace database administrators repairing source replication. 11. Linux, Docker, Kubernetes Linux delivery includes distributions, configuration, start/status/stop/upgrade procedures, and systemd. Docker includes pinned images, health checks, durable mounts, and credential injection. Declare x86 64/ARM64, JDK/driver, and native dependencies only after validation; Java bytecode portability does not prove native-library portability. Deliver both Helm Chart (values/schema, templates, upgrades, persistence options) and native YAML (applicable ConfigMaps, Secret references, Services, workloads, probes, RBAC, PVCs), usable with kubectl apply. Maintain both through the same configuration model and render/consistency checks. Test defaults/local volumes/external storage/HA/upgrades; screenshots or hand-written-resource instructions are insufficient. Local authoritative journals require recoverable volumes and single-writer policy; shared-journal workers may have no authoritative local state. Replica count is not safe takeover, and RWO is not fencing. Validate/version configuration/Secret changes. Graceful stop completes or rolls back the current safe unit and releases ownership. Separate liveness, readiness, and subscription status to avoid restart storms during source outages or pauses. Support private registries, offline dependencies/driver packages, and certificates. Cryptographic, OS/CPU, and vendor certifications require actual dependency/testing records; do not claim certification by default. 12. Hardware/performance standard Deliver benchmark tools, workload definitions, raw reports, and sizing guidance rather than invented rows-per-core figures. 4C/8GiB, 8C/16GiB, and 16C/32GiB may be experimental tiers , not measured throughput or production minimums. Record source, worker, journal, and each target's hardware separately. Record CPU model/architecture/quota, RAM/heap, disk type/capacity/measured bandwidth/IOPS/durability settings, network RTT/bandwidth, product/driver versions, tables/indexes, row width, JSON/LOB, identity class, transaction sizes, operation mix, target count, batches/concurrency, and acknowledgment policy. Measure snapshot rows/s and MiB/s, CDC events/s and transactions/s, end-to-end p50/p95/p99 latency, visibility delay, backlog growth, takeover/catch-up time, resource use, source business impact, and final validation. Separate keyless, fan-out, MQ, JSON, and transaction-size cases. Narrow single-table benchmarks cannot represent all deployments. For backlog B, incoming rate r, and apply capacity c in matching units, sustained catch-up requires c r; ideal catch-up time is B/(c-r). Journal sizing approximates durable log rate × required retention plus active snapshot artifacts, large-transaction staging, index/metadata space, and margin, adjusted for measured compression/write amplification. More hardware cannot remove hot-key ordering, source/target bottlenecks, or network limits. 13. Migration, parallel service, extensions Scenario Boundary and extension --- --- Online migration/read-only mirrors Snapshot+CDC, data/object reconciliation, secondary-constraint conversion, migration reports Both environments serving reads One authoritative writer; route reads according to table/target watermarks and explicit staleness budget Gradual/domain cutover Explicit table/domain ownership, application routing, cross-domain transaction boundaries; service does not silently change application endpoints Independent writers to the same table Requires bidirectional capture, conflict rules, origin/loop prevention, key allocation, repair; two opposing tasks are insufficient Failback after cutover Before new business writes, planned routing rollback may suffice; afterwards require verified reverse capture/compensation and validation Real-time warehouse/events ClickHouse/Doris/Hive and all seven messaging families with traceable events/schemas Application compatibility SQL/object assessment, read-only shadow queries, interface regression, performance reports; data migration does not automatically port application SQL Cutover gates include freezing relevant source writes/DDL, final barriers, target apply/visibility, data validation, restored constraints/generated behavior, synchronization fencing, and application handover. Open new writes only after required gates pass; do not promise automatic application changes or unconditional zero downtime. Extensions include lineage/audit, history/CDC archiving, data-quality rules, masked distribution, rehearsals, and capacity forecasts. Transformations/masking mark outputs as transformed, not exact mirrors. PostgreSQL/Oracle capture should be later connector milestones before corresponding reverse paths can be validated. Active-active conflict merging and cross-environment global transactions are separate advanced projects, not implied first-release guarantees. 14. Delivery sequence and completion Phase Delivery/acceptance --- --- P0 Foundation Rename, source-neutral events/positions/SPI, capability matrix, configuration versions, task/subscription isolation; preserve existing recovery regressions P1 Correctness/UI foundation Keyless/JSON/generated columns, baseline/DDL recovery, relational targets, wizard/incidents; object/transaction/fault matrix P2 Storage/distribution Three journals, fan-out, all in-scope MQ, ClickHouse/Doris/Hive; lost ACK/duplicates/reordering/partial batches/quotas P3 Migration closure Existing targets, validation/repair, constraint restoration, cutover gates/audit, Linux/Docker/Helm/native YAML, full bilingual manual P4 Performance/product acceptance Hardware benchmarks, soak/fault/upgrade matrix, security configuration/offline delivery; truthful status per target Later source milestones PostgreSQL/Oracle connectors and snapshot/long-transaction/failover acceptance before verified reverse paths Phasing does not demote in-scope message targets or objects to optional suggestions. Every stage delivers runnable functionality, matching UI, bilingual documentation, and fault tests. Do not mark design-only adapters available. Apache preparation separately includes name review, community/governance, ownership/dependency terms, LICENSE/NOTICE, reproducible builds, and test infrastructure. Rivomesh is not currently an Apache project. ASF naming.

title: PostgreSQL source
text: PostgreSQL source 中文 This experimental profile reads committed transactions from one writable PostgreSQL 17 or 18 primary using built-in pgoutput . Configure one source database per task. In this profile, databases lists source schemas. Declare destination mappings with targets[].mappings . Configure and run 1. Set wal level=logical and reserve slot capacity for the durable stream and an exported snapshot. Give the source role LOGIN , REPLICATION and SELECT on the published tables. 2. Create a publication that explicitly lists the synchronized tables and includes INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. Set REPLICA IDENTITY FULL on each table to retain full before images, including for keyless rows. Keep the publication scope stable and pause for review before schema changes. 3. Use the example configuration for the source, publication and destination. A PostgreSQL destination connection must be able to read pg control system() to verify physical identity. Configure distinct source and destination databases. 4. Run check config file to verify the connection and publication, then use run config file . In the management console, choose V3 → PostgreSQL in New task or import the V3 configuration. Enter one database, the source schemas, the publication and slot prefix. The wizard offers PostgreSQL and MySQL destinations. Save, run Check on the assigned Agent, then use Start . PostgreSQL supplies a consistent position when creating a logical replication slot. Rivomesh imports an exported MVCC snapshot for each table and captures concurrent transactions through the original LSN stream. It reports the flushed LSN only after journaling the complete transaction. Each task uses a slot bound to its journal generation. PostgreSQL replication protocol · pgJDBC replication API The PostgreSQL source uses pgJDBC 42.7.14 with automatic flush advancement disabled. Ordinary keepalives and WAL outside the publication leave the durable journal position unchanged. Monitor retained WAL during extended intervals without published transactions. pgJDBC download · Replication stream builder Profile and recovery - The initial type profile includes signed integers, booleans, bounded numeric values, text, JSON/JSONB and BYTEA. Keyed and keyless tables use full row identity. - PostgreSQL BYTEA maps to PostgreSQL BYTEA and MySQL LONGBLOB . The logical connection uses hex even when the source server defaults to escape . Use the native fixture with --source-image postgres:17.12 --bytea-values and add --bytea-escape-output for the second profile to verify SQL NULL , empty values, raw octets and keyless multiplicity during snapshot, CDC, and restart. The fixture also checks unchanged out-of-line TOAST values and 16–32 KiB payloads. PostgreSQL binary types - PostgreSQL UUID values are copied as lowercase canonical text in VARCHAR(36) . PostgreSQL 17.12 to PostgreSQL 17.12 verified nullable UUID values and primary-key changes through CDC. Reproduce with --uuid in the native fixture. PostgreSQL UUID representation - PostgreSQL DATE maps to DATE in both PostgreSQL and MySQL. The supported range is 1000-01-01 through 9999-12-31, and SQL NULL stays null. Snapshot and pgoutput use the same ISO representation. A civil date stays the same across Worker time zones and dates in the Gregorian calendar transition. PostgreSQL date and time · MySQL DATE range - PostgreSQL TIME WITHOUT TIME ZONE uses TIME(6) on PostgreSQL and MySQL targets, including the distinct 24:00:00 endpoint. Clock values retain microseconds and SQL NULL . TIMETZ remains unsupported. PostgreSQL date/time types · MySQL TIME precision - PostgreSQL timestamps with and without time zone use microsecond precision. A timestamp without time zone keeps its civil clock value, including civil times in a daylight-saving gap. A timestamp with time zone is copied as the equivalent UTC clock value. The PostgreSQL target stores TIMESTAMP(6) WITHOUT TIME ZONE and the MySQL target stores DATETIME(6) . Interpret the UTC column explicitly when a downstream application needs an instant. The shared range is 1000-01-01 00:00:00 through 9999-12-31 23:59:59.499999 . PostgreSQL timestamp semantics · MySQL DATETIME range - PostgreSQL 18 stored generated columns can be materialized as ordinary destination columns when the publication includes them. Use ALTER PUBLICATION rivomesh capture SET (publish generated columns=stored) and retain REPLICA IDENTITY FULL . PostgreSQL 17 generated columns, PostgreSQL 18 virtual generated columns, publication filters, partition routing, TRUNCATE and automatic DDL migration require separate profiles. Preflight or capture reports unsupported relation changes and types. - Restart uses the existing LSN and snapshot when the original primary, timeline, slot and journal remain available. Resume a failed target subscription after addressing its SQL error. - With POSTGRESQL REQUIRED WAL UNAVAILABLE , retain the old journal and record the last captured LSN. Evaluate whether the original slot and required WAL can be recovered. If needed, rebuild through a new pipeline and a reviewed destination scope. - SO-06 continues to track common-cut validation and additional target, promotion and driver profiles. Exact numeric values Source columns must declare a finite precision. PostgreSQL returns each value after applying its source precision and rounding rules. Rivomesh selects a target DECIMAL that fits every finite value in the declaration. Source declaration PostgreSQL and MySQL target storage Example --- --- --- NUMERIC(p,s) with 0 = s = p DECIMAL(p,s) NUMERIC(65,30) retains all 65 digits NUMERIC(p,s) with negative s DECIMAL(p + abs(s),0) NUMERIC(4,-2) uses DECIMAL(6,0) and copies the source-rounded integer NUMERIC(p,s) with s p DECIMAL(s,s) NUMERIC(2,4) uses DECIMAL(4,4) and copies the source's fractional values The shared profile allows up to 65 target digits and 30 fractional digits. These mappings preserve stored values, SQL NULL and row identities. PostgreSQL applies the original rounding and range to writes at the source. The target declaration can have a wider domain. The source adapter retains the original type modifier for its publication shape check. PostgreSQL numeric types · MySQL fixed-point types Preflight reports POSTGRESQL NUMERIC PRECISION REQUIRED for unconstrained NUMERIC and POSTGRESQL NUMERIC PROFILE UNSUPPORTED when the mapped precision or scale exceeds the profile. A non-finite value such as NaN causes POSTGRESQL NUMERIC NONFINITE . Capture holds its previous LSN and leaves the entire transaction unapplied. Preserve the slot and journal, then use the capture recovery review to confirm the retained checkpoint and affected subscriptions. A later source update does not remove the original transaction from WAL. Append --source-image postgres:17.12 --numeric-values to the fixture command below to verify PostgreSQL and MySQL snapshots, key changes, duplicate keyless updates and deletes, restart at the original LSN, and rejection of a transaction containing NaN . Floating-point types PostgreSQL REAL and DOUBLE PRECISION map to the same types on a PostgreSQL target and to FLOAT and DOUBLE on MySQL. Snapshot and pgoutput sessions select exact floating-point text. Native checks cover adjacent representable values, subnormals, SQL NULL, keyless duplicates and continuation after restart. Both signs of zero are copied as zero and share the same row identity. PostgreSQL floating-point types · MySQL floating-point types NaN and positive or negative infinity cause POSTGRESQL FLOAT NONFINITE . At the affected streaming transaction, capture holds its previous LSN, both target receipts and the business rows. Append --source-image postgres:17.12 --floating-values to the native fixture command. Verification Native verification commands Reproduce the native checks with python3 tests/postgres-source-run.py --artifact release jar --output target/pg-source-proof . The fixture simulates a lost PostgreSQL slot in disposable containers. Add --source-image postgres:17.12 --date-values to run the civil date fixture against PostgreSQL and MySQL destinations. It covers a DATE primary-key change, an exact keyless occurrence, restart from the original slot and snapshot, and refusal of an infinite date without applying its transaction. BCE dates and dates outside the profile range produce the same POSTGRESQL DATE OUT OF RANGE diagnostic. Review source values and the retained LSN before retrying. Add --source-image postgres:17.12 --timestamp-values to exercise both timestamp forms on the two SQL targets. The fixture checks DST boundaries, key changes, keyless duplicates, restart at the original LSN and refusal of the whole transaction when a timestamp yields POSTGRESQL TIMESTAMP OUT OF RANGE . Add --source-image postgres:17.12 --clock-values to verify both SQL destinations, the two midnight endpoints, keys, keyless rows, restart at the original LSN and preflight refusal of TIMETZ . Use Temurin 21 for current builds and fixtures. Earlier cross-runtime results are archived with their exact artifact. Verification record PostgreSQL 18.7 with PostgreSQL 17.12 as the destination passed eight Temurin 21 checks. The fixture covers stored generated values on keyed and keyless updates, materialization at the destination and omission from the publication. Add --source-image postgres:18 --generated to reproduce. Generated column publication Verified TLS connections Set the PostgreSQL source and destination JDBC URLs separately. Each can use sslmode=verify-full&sslrootcert=/run/rivomesh/trust/ca.pem&channelBinding=require when the server requires SCRAM with channel binding. Place the public CA certificate in the execution Agent's read-only filesystem. The DNS name in each URL must match the server certificate, including the stable writer name when using a database HA service. Run Check on the execution Agent after changing certificates or mounts. pgJDBC TLS · pgJDBC connection properties For the direct PostgreSQL 17.12 source and destination profile, add --source-image postgres:17.12 --tls to the native fixture. It generates temporary CAs and server certificates, inspects live TLS sessions and verifies that preflight refuses the wrong source hostname or target CA. PostgreSQL TLS statistics Synchronized standby promotion For a new task, keep one stable PostgreSQL writer endpoint in source.postgresql.url and set source.postgresql.failoverSlot: true . Equip the primary with a physical standby slot listed in synchronized standby slots . Configure the standby with that primary slot name , hot standby feedback=on , sync replication slots=on and a valid database name in primary conninfo . Verify that the logical slot on the standby is persistent, synchronized and has received the required WAL before routing a failover. PostgreSQL slot synchronization · Failover checklist The database HA service fences the previous primary, promotes the standby and routes the writer endpoint. Rivomesh reconnects through that endpoint. The promoted server must have the original system ID, an actual timeline history covering the durable LSN and snapshot coordinates, and the original failover slot. The slot must retain the required WAL and its confirmed LSN must not lead the journal. Retain the journal and old WAL if any of these checks fails. Configure the next physical standby before attempting another promotion. PostgreSQL 17.12 on Temurin 21 passed actual primary SIGKILL, native promotion, continued delivery with unchanged snapshot IDs, and refusal of a route back to the original timeline. The fixture checks the active timeline via IDENTIFY SYSTEM . Select --source-image postgres:17.12 --failover and append --reject-old-primary to run the divergent-route case. Load balancer products, cascading topologies and further version combinations have separate acceptance. Streaming replication protocol Review a paused schema change If a row transaction announces a changed relation through pgoutput, Rivomesh stops at the previous durable LSN with POSTGRESQL RELATION CHANGED REQUIRES PLAN . Open the capture failure review to compare the current publication against the journal schema. The read-only comparison shows table identity, recorded and current digests, and changed column names. A changed PostgreSQL type declaration, such as TIMESTAMP to TIMESTAMP(6) , is shown under modified columns. The view also flags relative reordering of existing columns. Treat it as an observation of the current publication. Later DDL can change the results because PostgreSQL pgoutput delivers relation metadata and row changes while DDL statements are outside the stream. A publication outside the supported profile returns the discovery diagnostic and retains the previous LSN. The review applies no DDL and makes no checkpoint changes. PostgreSQL logical replication restrictions · Relation messages Run the disposable native example with python3 tests/postgres-source-run.py --ddl-review --source-image postgres:17.12 --artifact release jar --output target/pg-ddl-review .

title: Reconciliation workflow
text: Data reconciliation, repair and a common cut The common barrier, MySQL consistent view, private disk staging, transactional SQL row comparison and CLI are implemented. The LOCAL/H2 and external PostgreSQL/MySQL/openGauss barrier profiles passed native acceptance; the newer row-comparison scope is recorded separately. The accepted CLI and UI repair profiles are described in the repair guide. Implemented foundation SourceAdapter.ConsistentRead represents one view across tables. Source-specific covers interprets position coverage; generic SourcePosition does not order GTID/LSN/SCN strings. MySQL uses GTID-set coverage. PipelineValidationBarrier.open(config, selectedTargets, maximumGateMillis, maximumReadMillis) checks the existing journal identity/running state/completed snapshots, obtains a bounded MySQL global read lock, establishes one REPEATABLE READ view and pins declared table metadata across configured databases. It records the source cut, waits for capture/normalization and selected target ACKs, then rechecks generation/epoch/position/sequence/snapshot acknowledgments under the journal job lock before persistently pausing and incrementing the epoch. Selected SQL targets acquire local transactional fences and must report the same sequence. JdbcSink.existing never creates lost checkpoint metadata. The source write gate is released while its MVCC view remains available for table reads. Unselected targets can be paused or offline; they are not presented as validated. The certificate contains source/capture positions, configuration fingerprint, generation, epoch, sequence, error version, schema hashes and selected target checkpoints. It proves a synchronization boundary, not row equality. Concurrent control or checkpoint changes invalidate eligibility. Source writes may continue after gate release; the task stays paused until explicit recovery processes later binlog events. Bounds and recovery The explicit source-gate limit is1–120seconds; the read session has a separate limit, at least as long and at most24hours. Deadlines abort owned connections, with session wait timeout as an additional cleanup measure. No global settings are changed. Network failures prevent an exact millisecond guarantee of server-side unlock; monitor database sessions as well. The source MVCC transaction holds table metadata locks and old row versions, which can delay DDL and grow undo. Native tests observe actual lock waits and release. Early closure of an unfinished cursor aborts the entire validation view instead of draining an unbounded result or treating a partial scan as complete. SIGKILL releases connections; durable pause cannot be bypassed by restart. Lost MVCC views cannot be reconstructed from files; incomplete source scans need a new cut. Fence failure retains the persisted pause. The protocol assumes a consistent writable destination endpoint and does not replace database HA routing/old-primary isolation. Selected destinations currently use transactional SQL. MQ producer acknowledgement is not downstream data validation; analytical visibility/materialization requires product-specific support. Primary MySQL references: consistent snapshots, FLUSH, session timeouts. Row comparison and CLI The synchronizer must be the only writer of destination business tables. Begin with a RUNNING pipeline, completed snapshots and selected targets able to reach the common cut. Establishing the cut briefly blocks writes across the MySQL instance. After releasing source writes, the pipeline stays PAUSED until explicitly resumed. CLI defaults:30second source gate,1hour source view,10minutes per destination table,1GiB logical staging budget and4MiB per row. Java callers can set explicit limits. Source rows, target rows and keyless identity records all consume the budget; it is not a1GiB source-data allowance. Physical-file checks run at batch commit boundaries; H2 pages/indexes/temporary data can require additional space. Use filesystem/container quotas for a hard physical limit. Large-scale capacity remains unaccepted. The source scan uses the original MVCC view. Keyless occurrence IDs are paged from the durable journal and matched against the complete canonical source multiset. Only complete source scans are sealed. Supported POSIX systems use0700directories/0600files, with same-process and cross-process writer locks. Staging is not encrypted; place it on appropriately private storage. Each destination scan holds the physical checkpoint row lock on the same connection used for reading. Ownership, schema, completed snapshot and exact checkpoint are checked without recreating metadata, advancing sequence or modifying business rows. Types share the synchronization canonicalization contract. Keyless internal identities are compared as well as values; equal data with wrong identities yields missing and extra differences. MySQL TIME expressions are explicitly cast to CHAR for source snapshots, consistent views, virtual-generated evaluation and target validation. This avoids JDBC temporal formatting losing a negative subsecond sign: -00:00:00.000001 must remain negative one microsecond. MySQL FLOAT32 targets explicitly use FLOAT; default-mode REAL aliases DOUBLE, as documented in the official numeric type reference. Existing incorrect table types need an explicit migration plan; validation never alters them automatically. Per-target/table results contain counts, content roots and missing , extra , changed totals. Equal results produce VALIDATION MATCH , otherwise VALIDATION DIFFERENCES . The Java store supports identity-hash keyset pages of up to200differences. Summaries omit business row values; raw values in private staging remain sensitive. Recovery boundaries: - A lost MySQL gate or snapshot session invalidates an incomplete source scan even if the driver reconnects to the same server. Inspect the durable pause, explicitly resume as appropriate and establish a new cut. - Once source data is sealed, validate-compare checks configuration/generation/epoch/error version/positions and physical target checkpoints, validates the source seal and row checksums, discards partial destination scans and rereads them. The source database need not be online during this phase. - Resuming/reconfiguring the pipeline or changing checkpoints invalidates continued comparison. Historical reports remain readable and do not prove current equality. - Success, failure and timeout all retain the pause. Use the current error version with the existing status / resume-pipeline controls to resume explicitly. The first end-to-end native comparison profile uses MySQL8.4 sources and PostgreSQL17/MySQL8.4 destinations. Other transactional adapters share the reader interface but their vendor/version/mode/distributed acceptance remains separate. Messaging and analytical destinations do not yet implement this comparison protocol. FAQ - Why did replication stop advancing after validation? Establishing the cut durably pauses it. Review the report/task state and explicitly resume using the current error version. Monitor source binlog retention and journal capacity while paused. - Can a longer timeout resume an incomplete source scan? A lost MySQL MVCC transaction cannot be reconstructed. Keep the failed report, follow explicit task recovery and establish a new cut with an appropriate read budget. - Why can equal keyless business values still produce missing/extra rows? Incorrect occurrence IDs break later UPDATE/DELETE processing. Counts or business-value-only comparison would miss this. - Can I rewrite hashes after VALIDATION SOURCE SEAL MISMATCH ? Do not alter the summary/H2 contents to force acceptance. It can indicate corruption, changed data or a development-era report format difference. Retain evidence and establish a new validation run; historical summaries remain useful for diagnosis. - Did validation repair rows or rebuild UNIQUE constraints? Validation reads destinations. Use the managed repair workflow for reviewed row changes and verify constraints before handover. Recovery runbook Record the task ID, configuration revision, capture position, error generation, affected subscriptions and request ID. The V3 capture position covers complete source transactions retained in the journal. Each target's acknowledgment covers its acknowledged prefix. When a skip has opened a gap, compare the open gaps, contiguous applied position and safe covered position. Use the observation time to establish how recent each displayed state is. The console keeps operation history. API writes use POST /api/tasks/ task /actions with expectedRevision and X-Request-ID . Browser sessions also use CSRF tokens. Use the task or subscription errorCount specified by the corresponding workflow. If a response is lost, look up that request or retry with the same ID and body. Inspect command admission and the actual commit separately. Symptom and cause Console or API action Checkpoints, gaps and retries --- --- --- MySQL primary changes or replication IO/SQL stops Inspect the connection stage and candidate topology. Have the database operator fence the old primary, repair replication, promote an eligible primary and confirm retained GTID history. Rivomesh reconnects at the durable GTID. Lag, replica failure or multiple writable candidates leave the original checkpoint in place until an eligible source is available. See source failover. Missing MySQL binlog, PostgreSQL slot or WAL, or a decoding failure Open Review capture recovery as an administrator or call GET /api/tasks/ task /capture-recovery . Recover the logs or select a source with the required history. Review a new baseline if the logs are unavailable. The read-only review preserves the old position and lists every potentially affected subscription. Keep the error paused while the source range is unproved. See capture recovery. A reviewable MySQL decoder fault Retain the original transaction, verify its exact GTID and destinations, then approve the source skip for an eligible keyed row transaction. The task remains paused and both target ACKs remain unchanged. Resume later changes separately and reconcile the recorded source gap. Source skip Target SQL, permission or constraint error Find the failed subscription, resolve the native error and use RESUME TARGET for that subscription. Healthy subscriptions can continue. Use its current error generation. The same transaction replays at the original position. SQL data and the native receipt commit together. Target commit succeeded and its journal acknowledgment or response was lost Pause the task, retain the failure evidence and inspect the native receipt. Use the administrator confirmation workflow or CONFIRM COMMIT for a supported profile. Reconcile the acknowledgment for that exact transaction. Preserve the committed rows. Explicitly resume the task and subscription after review. See commit acknowledgment. Controller or Agent goes offline while a command is pending Inspect the owner, observation time and operation result from an available controller. In the fixed-Agent profile, a durable STOP request can wait for the original Agent. A live Worker can continue against its journal. An unreachable owner shows unknown state. Check the persisted request after restart. Verify journal, keys and target identity before relocation. See global control. Local volume or external journal is unavailable, or quota is exhausted Inspect the journal storage stage. Restore the original volume or external store, check generation, durable position and native receipts, then restart. Review transaction size and capacity for quota failures. Preserve the journal, configuration, snapshot artifacts and receipts. Rebuild a reviewed baseline when the original journal cannot be restored. See deployment and storage. Browser refresh, session revocation or changed permissions A normal refresh uses a valid session. Sign in again after expiration or revocation. Administrators can revoke sessions through their account and session controls. Session state leaves data checkpoints unchanged. After signing in, use the same operation ID to inspect work in progress. See browser sessions. A complete failed transaction needs exclusion Have an administrator review evidence, target scope and reason, then use target transaction skipping. Check the native SKIP receipt before resuming. Exclude the complete next transaction for that subscription and retain the explicit gap. Safe coverage can advance while contiguous applied progress retains the earlier boundary. See transaction skip and gap verification. Repair rows or undo target effects of a failed transaction Review before/after values, scope and the receipt hash. Choose before-image compensation or a typed correction. Record execute and cancel requests against the original operation. Write corrections and receipts atomically, then retain the pause. Replay the original event after compensation. Recheck the gap and original position after a correction. Check the original result after cancellation. See compensation and manual correction. Relational, analytical and messaging targets report product-specific progress. A broker acknowledgment confirms acceptance by the broker. Verify application or persistence using the downstream system. Native SQL receipts, compensation and gap verification follow the accepted profiles in the linked guides. Cutover and fallback For an initial comparison of existing MySQL data in a PostgreSQL target, use the existing target preview. Keep the source authoritative for business writes and let Rivomesh write the targets. Pause business writes for the final cut, establish a fresh common boundary, compare destination content and downstream visibility, and restore business constraints before handing over writes. Revalidate UNIQUE or GSI constraints that were represented as ordinary indexes against the target product. Historical reports retain the earlier results. Validate the new business state and a fallback baseline separately after cutover. Nonempty target adoption, automatic Agent takeover and cross-product constraint recovery follow their explicit acceptance profiles. 中文

title: Recovery & consistency
text: V2 recovery, primary failover and consistency 中文：恢复、主库切换与一致性. This document describes the v2 single-database, single-target core . V3 uses MVCC snapshot artifacts, a separate journal and independent destinations: follow the V3 manual and message contract. V2 state cannot be adopted simply by setting formatVersion: 3 . Service ownership Processes create v2 metadata idempotently, handling concurrent catalog creation separately. Initial task configuration and discovered-table manifests are inserted atomically. Conditional updates claim the owner and lease; a separate heartbeat renews the lease, and data/progress transactions check the same owner. Each new work session uses a new owner identity so callbacks from an older replication connection cannot commit into the new session. The task-row lock serializes capture, snapshot and application commits. After ownership transfers, the old owner is rejected before business writes and cannot pause or release the new owner's task. Standby nodes do not open binlog connections; a healthy task normally has one replication client. Persistent GTID state - capture gtid : the initial baseline plus committed source transactions durably queued or irrelevant to the selected business database. - required gtid : the union of captured transactions and the GTIDs required by source state already read during snapshot/discovery. - applied sequence : the queued transaction sequence already applied to business tables. Physical UUIDs and file positions support diagnostics and backend validation; cross-server recovery uses GTIDs. A complete source commit is persisted before adding its GTID to capture gtid . The connector's possibly earlier in-memory GTID is never copied directly over persistent progress. Duplicate GTIDs are checked under the task lock and do not enqueue the same durable transaction twice. Primary failover during a snapshot After recording baseline B0, capture FULL row images while scanning by primary-key cursor. Every chunk records a source GTID watermark after reading; its business rows, last key and read dependency commit together. Discovery and initial scan-upper-bound reads also contribute to required gtid . A snapshot may have read a transaction from the former primary before the capture connection persisted it. Validating only capture gtid would miss that dependency. A failover candidate must therefore include required gtid . After all chunks complete, record B1, wait until capture gtid includes B1, then replay the queue in source commit order. The scan imports unchanged rows; the final full row image or DELETE establishes the result for changed rows. Primary-key changes remove the old key and write the new key. Logs cover inserts before the scan cursor and beyond the initial upper bound. During snapshot and early replay, the target is not a consistent image of one source instant. During continuous incremental application, every source transaction, including cross-table changes, is applied in one destination transaction. This v2 cursor approach differs from v3's restart/rebase of an incomplete MVCC snapshot. Primary discovery and selection 1. Probe candidate addresses for UUID, server id, read-only state, GTID mode, executed/purged sets and replication health. 2. In ordinary primary/replica topologies, select only a writable node without active upstream threads or residual replication errors. 3. For Group Replication, require ONLINE, PRIMARY, writable and single-primary mode. 4. Multiple writable primaries require external isolation; the service does not arbitrarily choose one. 5. Require required gtid ⊆ candidate.gtid executed ; otherwise wait for catch-up. 6. Require candidate.gtid purged ⊆ capture gtid ; otherwise necessary uncaptured history may already be unavailable, so block progress. 7. Reconnect with persistent GTID auto-positioning. Automatic fallback to the purged set is disabled. JDBC queries validate physical UUID and writability; the replication connection validates its handshake server id before processing events. If a router/VIP sends these connections to different backends, abandon the session and rediscover. Heartbeat expiry, disconnection or source role changes also establish a new session from persistent GTIDs. Operators must ensure candidates belong to the same logical topology, replicate all selected data, and have no filtering or forged GTIDs. Equal GTID sets cannot detect every manual data modification. CDC cannot reconstruct permanently lost asynchronous transactions that never reached a surviving candidate. Rivomesh does not promote MySQL nodes.
